Urban data scientist in San Diego

Hi, I’m Jhoven (Johan) Fernandez.

My research is on GeoAI: what the term means, how it differs from ordinary AI run on map data, and how location-aware AI could shape infrastructure planning and the way cities are designed. I use data science, machine learning and spatial analysis to ask who benefits when a model helps decide where public money goes. I think a city should only trust a model’s ranking when the evidence behind it is clear, and so is its effect on residents.

I’m applying to PhD programs in New York City, where I’d like to build GeoAI methods that cities can check and explain. My work so far is in my research series, GeoAI for Cities, and in my projects.

GeoAI for Cities, exploratory research

Manhattan, Measured

A walk through two centuries of spatial research in New York, from the 1811 street grid to FireCast. Almost none of it was called GeoAI at the time.

The term GeoAI showed up in 2017, but people in New York were using maps, cameras, GPS records and models to decide where to build, inspect and protect long before that. Scroll and the drone follows the route. Each stop is one dated case, with what was done, what it found and what was left open. The stops are in street order, so the timeline under the map lists them by year.

Scroll down to start

The stops, in route order

  1. One Police Plaza, 1994: CompStat turned pin maps of subway robberies into weekly mapped crime statistics.
  2. Houston Street, 1811: the Commissioners’ Plan laid 12 avenues and 155 streets over the island.
  3. Flatiron Building, 2013–2014: Place Pulse and Streetscore learned perceived safety from street images.
  4. Empire State Building, 2011: risk scoring raised the share of inspections ending in a vacate order from 13% to 70%.
  5. Times Square, 2009: taxi GPS showed northbound trips 17% faster and motorist injuries down 63% after the Broadway plazas.
  6. Bryant Park, 1968: the RAND fire models, and the fires of the 1970s.
  7. Grand Central Terminal, 2013: FireCast scores about 350,000 buildings for fire risk.
  8. Seagram Building plaza, 1969–1980: William H. Whyte filmed plazas and counted how people used them.
  9. Central Park, 2010: the Green Infrastructure Plan set targets to cut sewer overflows by more than 12 billion gallons a year.

Timeline

Ten cases over about two centuries. The last column shows that most of the questions GeoAI now automates were being asked long before there were methods to answer them at scale.

Case studies

Each case in more detail, including what we still don't know.

1811, Houston Street

The 1811 grid as an early spatial model

What happened
A state commission of Gouverneur Morris, John Rutherfurd and Simeon De Witt adopted a plan of 12 avenues, 100 feet wide, and 155 cross streets, creating about 2,000 long, narrow blocks. John Randel Jr. surveyed it.1
Reasoning
The commissioners chose right angles because “straight-sided and right-angled houses are the most cheap to build and the most convenient to live in.”
Why it matters now
Every New York dataset, from tax lots to sensor feeds, is shaped by this grid, so any spatial model of Manhattan carries part of an 1811 decision inside it.

1968 onward, citywide (Bryant Park stop)

The RAND fire models

What happened
In 1968 New York began working with the RAND Corporation on computer modeling of city services, starting with the Fire Department. Over the next decade the models informed the closing and relocation of fire companies.2
What it found
Journalist Joe Flood argues the cuts withdrew protection from the poorest neighborhoods, including the Bronx, Harlem, the Lower East Side and parts of Brooklyn, as fires surged. In his account the fires of the 1970s displaced more than 600,000 people.2
Limits of the evidence
This is a journalist’s reconstruction, and it hasn't been tested in a controlled study. Other causes of the fires are still debated.
Lesson for GeoAI
A model that allocates protection is also deciding who gets it. It can be accurate on average and still put most of its mistakes on certain neighborhoods.

1969 to 1980, Seagram Building plaza

Counting people on film

What happened
William H. Whyte’s Street Life Project, begun in 1969 for the City Planning Commission, filmed plazas with time-lapse cameras and counted how people used them.3,4
What it found
Use depended on simple things you could measure. Places to sit mattered most, followed by sun, trees, water and food. The city’s plaza rules came to require seating, including one linear foot for every 30 square feet of plaza.4
Published as
The book and film The Social Life of Small Urban Spaces (1980).
Lesson for GeoAI
Detecting and counting people in public space is now a standard computer-vision task. Whyte's work is a reminder to decide what to count, and why, before building the counter.

1994, One Police Plaza

CompStat and weekly crime maps

What happened
Jack Maple, then with the Transit Police, tracked subway robberies with pins on wall maps he called the “Charts of the Future.” As an NYPD deputy commissioner from 1994 he built CompStat, a system of weekly meetings organized around mapped crime statistics.5
What followed
Versions of CompStat spread to most large U.S. police departments.
Open question
Mapped incidents reflect both where events happen and where they are reported and recorded. Any model trained on complaints or 311 calls has the same problem.

2009, Times Square

Using taxi GPS to evaluate Green Light for Midtown

What happened
The city closed parts of Broadway to cars around Times Square as a pilot, in place from late May to mid-August 2009.6
Data and method
The Department of Transportation compared fall 2008 and fall 2009 travel times using GPS records from about 1.13 million taxi trips in West Midtown and 890,000 in East Midtown.6
What it found
Northbound trips in West Midtown were 17% faster, while southbound trips were 2% slower. Injuries to motorists and passengers fell 63%, pedestrian injuries 35%, and 80% fewer pedestrians walked in the roadway in Times Square. The changes were made permanent.6
Lesson for GeoAI
Location data a city already collects for other reasons can be used to check an investment after it's built.

2010, Central Park

The 2010 Green Infrastructure Plan and its targets

What happened
In September 2010 New York released its Green Infrastructure Plan. About two-thirds of the city’s sewered area is served by combined sewers, which overflow into waterways in heavy rain.7
Targets
Capture the first inch of rain on 10% of impervious surfaces in combined-sewer areas, cutting overflows by more than 12 billion gallons a year by 2030, a 40% reduction, for $5.3 billion against $6.8 billion for an all-grey plan.7
Lesson for GeoAI
A citywide target eventually has to turn into a list of specific sites. Deciding which blocks go first is the ranking question this series looks at.

2011, citywide (Empire State Building stop)

Scoring buildings for hidden risk

What happened
After fires in illegally converted buildings in 2011 injured and killed firefighters, the Mayor’s Office of Policy and Strategic Planning analytics team, led by Michael Flowers, studied which complaints led to vacate orders.8
Data and method
It combined building violations, foreclosures, tax liens, 311 complaints, building age and neighborhood conditions to rank incoming complaints.8
What it found
Inspectors had found conditions bad enough to vacate a building 13% of the time; with the ranking, they found them 70% of the time.8
Limits of the evidence
The figures come from press accounts of the city’s own results. They haven't been checked by an independent evaluation.

2013, citywide (Grand Central stop)

FireCast and predictive fire inspection

What happened
The FDNY introduced risk-based inspection, with FireCast scoring about 350,000 buildings so inspectors visit the riskiest first.9,10
Data and method
Building-level risk scores built from several city agencies' data streams. A later version planned to use some 7,500 factors from 17 streams.9
Lesson for GeoAI
Decades after RAND, the same city built a much richer model. Whether anyone audits who it protects is still the open question from the RAND years.

2013 to 2014, Flatiron Building

Rating streets from photographs

What happened
MIT’s Place Pulse asked volunteers to compare pairs of street images from New York, Boston and two Austrian cities.11 Streetscore then trained a model on the judgments of more than 7,000 participants and scored about one million Street View images across 21 U.S. cities.12
What it shows
A model can learn from photographs whether people see a street as safe or unsafe, and the results can be mapped block by block.
Open question
It's not clear whose perception the model is learning. Ratings from one group of volunteers may not match how residents see their own blocks.

2014, Times Square

Testing taxi pooling on 150 million trips

What happened
Researchers built “shareability networks” from more than 150 million New York taxi trips taken in 2011.13
What it found
With modest extra travel time for passengers, total trip length could be cut by 40% or more.13
Lesson for GeoAI
Open city data made it possible to put a number and a map on a policy idea, years before anyone used the term GeoAI.

Open questions

This walk is exploratory, and it leaves a lot unsettled. These are the questions I'd most like to work on.

  • Where the data come from. CompStat, 311 and the 2011 complaint ranking all start from reports. When does mapped data show where problems are, and when does it show where people looked?
  • Who audits allocation. RAND and FireCast both decide where protection goes. What would a fair audit of a spatial ranking look like?
  • Whose perception. Place Pulse learned how volunteers saw streets. Would residents rank their own blocks the same way?
  • Evaluation after the fact. Taxi GPS evaluated Times Square. Which other passive data could test whether a city investment delivered?
  • Value and need. Green infrastructure can be ranked by gallons captured per dollar, or by benefit to the blocks that flood most. Which should come first, and who decides?

About

Urban data science and GeoAI, based in San Diego

My research is about who gets what in cities.

When a city can only plant trees, fix streets or fund drainage projects in a few places each year, someone has to decide which neighborhoods go first. I want to know how those rankings get built, whether the data behind them holds up, and who keeps ending up at the bottom of the list.

Where the question came from

On stormwater programs for four cities, I kept the geodatabases that ranked Capital Improvement Plan sites. A fixed set of weights decided which projects moved first.

At the American Academy of Pediatrics I joined Census data to infrastructure layers and kept finding the same neighborhoods short on services.

At UC San Diego I studied Logan Heights and City Heights, where decisions about freeways and housing were often made without much input from the people who live there.

What I'm testing now

GeoAI, meaning machine learning that pays attention to location, could make those rankings fairer, or it could just make them faster and harder to question. My projects test that with public data:

  • Who Gets the Shade?Which New York neighborhoods a tree program would reach first
  • Will It Get Built?Which San Diego housing sites are likely to see homes
  • CurbCallHow residents might rank street repairs themselves

That's the work I want to keep doing in graduate school in New York.

Part 2 of 3, about a 9-minute read

GeoAI for Cities, Part 2. Original study, working paper (October 2026)

Who Gets the Shade? Ranking New York Neighborhoods for Tree Planting

Cities rank neighborhoods to decide where public money goes first. I used public data for all 42 of New York’s health neighborhoods to ask how much the choice of ranking rule changes who benefits, and how well a model of heat illness holds up outside the places it was trained on.

By Jhoven (Johan) Fernandez. The code and data are on GitHub, and there is an interactive map. This paper covers research question 3 of the series.

Key findings

  • Neighborhoods with more tree canopy were cooler: about 0.17 °F lower surface temperature per percentage point of canopy (R² = 0.42).
  • Heat illness tracked poverty (r = 0.59) far more than surface temperature (r = 0.20).
  • The ranking rule changed who benefits. Ranking by canopy gap put 4 of the top 10 in the poorest third of neighborhoods; an equity-weighted rule put 9.
  • A model that looked useful under ordinary testing (R² = 0.24) failed when asked to predict a borough it had not seen (R² = -0.27).

1. The question

Every tree-planting program has to decide where to start, and that decision is a ranking. In Part 1 I argued that the step from “predict” to “decide” has the least evidence behind it. Here I test that step with two questions:

  1. Distribution. If a city ranks neighborhoods by heat, by missing canopy, by heat illness, or by a combined score, how different are the neighborhoods that come first, and who lives there?
  2. Transfer. Can a model that predicts heat illness from heat, greenery and poverty be trusted in a borough it was not trained on?

2. Data

The unit of analysis is the United Hospital Fund neighborhood. All five variables and the boundary files are public and come from the city health department (Table 1).

Table 1. Variables. All five come from the NYC Department of Health Environment & Health Data Portal, for the 42 United Hospital Fund (UHF) neighborhoods.

VariableMeasureYearCitywide mean
Surface temperatureDaytime summer land-surface temperature from Landsat thermal imagery, °F18 Aug 200994.2 °F
Tree canopyTree canopy as % of land area201419.2%
Vegetative coverAll vegetation as % of land area201030.1%
PovertyResidents below 100% of the federal poverty level, %2013–17 (ACS)19.2%
Heat illnessHeat-stress emergency department visits, age-adjusted per 100,000, averaged over years2005–20147.6

The portal files Bensonhurst–Bay Ridge under Canarsie–Flatlands’ code, so a naive join silently drops a neighborhood. I re-keyed the data by name instead. An independent re-computation is what caught the error.

3. Methods

  • Spatial clustering. Global Moran’s I for each variable and local indicators of spatial association (LISA) for surface temperature, with five-nearest-neighbor weights (the Rockaways have no land neighbor) and 9,999 permutations.
  • Regression. Ordinary least squares with residual diagnostics, compared with spatial lag and spatial error models.
  • Validation. Linear regression and random forest predicting heat illness, scored by repeated random five-fold cross-validation and by leave-one-borough-out cross-validation.
  • Ranking. Five rules for choosing ten priority neighborhoods (Table 3). The equity-weighted score is the mean of standardized surface temperature, canopy gap, heat illness and poverty. I tested its stability with 5,000 random weightings of the four inputs.

4. Results

Shade and heat

Surface temperature, canopy, poverty and heat illness were all spatially clustered (Moran’s I 0.27 to 0.43, all p < 0.01). Canopy explained about 43% of surface temperature; a spatial error model put the effect at 0.18 °F per point of canopy, close to the ordinary estimate (Table 2, Figure 2).

Table 2. Regression results (ordinary least squares, n = 42). Residual Moran’s I tests whether the errors are still clustered in space.

ModelKey coefficientpR²Residual Moran’s I
Surface temp ~ canopy-0.174 °F per point of canopy< 0.0010.420.35 (p = 0.0002)
Surface temp ~ canopy, spatial error model-0.183 °F per point; λ = 0.63AIC 151.6 vs 162.8Accounted for
Heat ED visits ~ surface temp + povertyPoverty 0.239 per point; surface temp -0.214< 0.001; 0.370.370.18 (p = 0.017)

Heat and illness

Heat illness tracked poverty much more closely than temperature. Each point of poverty added about 0.24 emergency visits per 100,000 (p < 0.001), while temperature added nothing measurable (p = 0.37). Hotter places were also poorer (r = 0.51). I don't read this as heat being harmless. It looks more like who is exposed, and whether they have air conditioning and good health, matters more than small temperature differences between neighborhoods.

Each ranking rule picks different neighborhoods

The rules disagreed (Figure 4, Table 3). The canopy-gap rule favors Manhattan (Chelsea–Clinton, Greenwich Village–SoHo, Gramercy–Murray Hill) and the Rockaways, which are heavy on beach. The heat-illness rule favors northern Staten Island. Their top tens shared only 2 of 10, and across all 42 their ranks were unrelated (Spearman ρ = -0.02).

Table 3. Five rules for choosing the ten neighborhoods to plant first, and who each rule reaches. Citywide: poverty 19.2%, heat ED rate 7.6, surface temperature 94.2 °F, canopy 19.2%.

RuleTop of its listIn poorest thirdMean povertyMean heat ED rateMean surface tempMean canopy
Heat-first: hottest surfacesHunts Point - Mott Haven, Williamsburg - Bushwick, High Bridge - Morrisania…6 of 1024.7%9.4896.68 °F13.8%
Canopy-gap: least canopyHunts Point - Mott Haven, Chelsea - Clinton, Greenpoint…4 of 1021.5%7.3695.77 °F10.6%
Health-need: most heat illnessPort Richmond, Williamsburg - Bushwick, East Harlem…7 of 1028.4%12.6495.29 °F17.6%
Equity-weighted: all four, equal weightHunts Point - Mott Haven, Williamsburg - Bushwick, East Harlem…9 of 1030.5%11.0596.53 °F14.1%
Need-weighted: heat, canopy, illness (no poverty)Williamsburg - Bushwick, Hunts Point - Mott Haven, East Harlem…8 of 1028.0%11.1996.48 °F13.5%

Even without poverty as an input, the equity rule placed 8 of 10 in the poorest third. Six neighborhoods made the top ten under at least 90% of 5,000 random weightings: Bedford Stuyvesant - Crown Heights, East Harlem, East New York, High Bridge - Morrisania, Hunts Point - Mott Haven, Williamsburg - Bushwick. I treat these as robust priorities, since they stay near the top whatever the weights.

Prediction in a borough the model hasn't seen

When I held out random neighborhoods, the model explained about a quarter of heat illness. When I held out a whole borough, it did worse than the city average (Table 4, Figure 6), and worst on Staten Island. Random testing leaked information from neighboring areas, which is the problem Part 1 warned about.

Table 4. Prediction accuracy for heat-related ED visits, from surface temperature, canopy, vegetation and poverty.

ModelRandom 5-fold CV, R²Leave-one-borough-out CV, R²Error on Staten Island when held out
Linear regression0.24 (± 0.05)-0.276.4 visits per 100,000
Random forest0.10 (± 0.05)-0.055.3 visits per 100,000

5. What this means for cities

  • Treat the ranking rule as a policy decision. Ranking by canopy gap or by heat illness decides which communities are served first, so it is more than a technical detail. I think cities should publish the rule they use and show who it reaches.
  • Start with the robust priorities. Six neighborhoods rank near the top under almost any weighting, so starting there is defensible whatever weights the council settles on.
  • Test models where they will be used. A heat-illness model should be validated on areas it has not seen before it guides spending elsewhere.

6. Limitations

  • Ecological, cross-sectional data. Neighborhood averages cannot show what happens to individuals, and associations are not effects. Canopy was measured in 2014, after much of the illness data, so this is not evidence that planting reduces illness.
  • Coarse geography. Forty-two neighborhoods hide large differences within them; results may change at block or tract level (the modifiable areal unit problem in Part 1).
  • One summer image. Surface temperature comes from a single Landsat scene from August 2009, and it measures surfaces, which can differ a lot from the air temperature people feel.
  • Averaged illness rates. Heat illness is a simple average of yearly age-adjusted rates, which swing widely with summer weather.
  • Missing drivers. I didn't model air-conditioning access, age or health conditions, which are the factors behind the city’s own Heat Vulnerability Index.

7. Next steps

Next I plan to work at the census-tract level with current canopy data and more Landsat scenes, add air-conditioning and age data, and try rankings that learn from outcomes such as illness after planting (research question 2).

Data and sources

  1. New York City Department of Health and Mental Hygiene. Environment & Health Data Portal, public data export. github.com/nycehs/All_EHDP_Data
  2. NYC DOHMH. NYC geography boundary files (UHF 42). github.com/nycehs/NYC_geography
  3. Anselin, L. (1995). Local indicators of spatial association: LISA. Geographical Analysis, 27(2), 93–115.
  4. Roberts, D. R., et al. (2017). Cross-validation strategies for data with temporal, spatial, hierarchical, or phylogenetic structure. Ecography, 40(8), 913–929.

    GeoAI for Cities, Part 3. Original study, working paper (October 2026)

    Record Heat, Record Demand: Can GeoAI Predict Where the Grid Strains?

    In September 2026, San Diego’s grid hit its highest demand on record. I used utility meter data for 3.9 million households in New York and San Diego to see where summer electricity use climbs, what explains it, and whether a model built in one place can predict another.

    By Jhoven (Johan) Fernandez. Builds on Part 2: Who Gets the Shade? The code, data and a note on how each dataset was pulled are on GitHub.

    Key findings

    • In summer, New York homes use 67% more electricity than in spring and fall (Con Edison ZIP data, 2024–2025). San Diego homes use 23% more (SDG&E, 2019).
    • In San Diego, summer demand rises with distance from the ocean. ZIP codes more than 30 km inland add three to six times as much summer electricity per account as coastal ones, depending on which summer months are compared.
    • In New York, the neighborhoods with the hottest surfaces, which are also the densest, add less summer power per account, not more. Home size and housing type explain Con Edison’s peak allocation far better than surface heat (74% of the variation against 32%).
    • Across the largest cities, summer adds the most in Phoenix (793 extra kWh per account each month, roughly $360 a summer) and the least in Los Angeles (33 kWh, about $24). New York’s high prices push its summer increase to about $206, more than Chicago’s.
    • Can GeoAI predict where the grid strains? Only partly. Models captured broad differences between areas, but on a New York borough they had not seen, most scored near zero or worse, and all failed on Staten Island. In San Diego, a tree-based model trained near the coast could not predict beyond the range of distances it had seen, while a simple straight-line trend did much better.

    1. Why this matters now

    Heat costs money twice. Households pay for the extra air conditioning, and utilities have to build a grid big enough for the hottest days, even though those days are few. When the grid can’t keep up, the cost lands on everyone.

    San Diego, September and October 2026

    On September 9, SDG&E’s demand reached 5,209 megawatts, as reported by the San Diego Union-Tribune. The utility’s previous record was 5,032 megawatts, set in September 2024. Between September 8 and 9, nearly 15,000 customers lost power in 29 unplanned outages. In early October the airport set daily highs of 95°F, 105°F and 100°F, recorded six straight days at or above 90°F, and posted record-warm nights.

    Queens, July 2006

    During a heat wave, Con Edison kept the network running after 10 of its 22 feeder cables had failed, overloading the remaining 12. About 174,000 people were affected, many for about a week, and business losses ran to tens of millions of dollars. Con Edison’s decision to keep the overloaded network running was the main cause; the heat added load.

    Sacramento, summer 2007

    A U.S. Forest Service study used real utility bills from 460 homes. Trees on a house’s west and south sides cut summer electricity use by about 5% on average. Trees on the north side raised it, and trees on the east side made no measurable difference.

    New York City, 2017

    Cool Neighborhoods NYC put $106 million into cooling the city, including $82 million for street trees, aimed at neighborhoods most vulnerable on the city’s Heat Vulnerability Index. The city’s report notes that the urban heat island drives higher summer peak energy demand.

    Who this is for

    Utilities and grid plannersWhich neighborhoods drive the summer peak, and what predicts them.
    Investors and insurersHow much of a heat-risk score survives outside the place it was built.
    City agenciesWhether tree money also lowers energy demand, and by how much.
    Researchers and data scientistsA public, repeatable test of spatial models on unseen places.

    2. The questions

    1. Where does each city use the most extra electricity in summer? Measured per account, so large and small ZIP codes compare fairly.
    2. What explains it: heat, shade, income or housing?
    3. Can GeoAI predict where the grid strains? Tested on places the model never saw: a New York borough held out of training, and inland San Diego predicted from the coast.

    3. Data

    Table 1. All sources are public.
    MeasureSourceDetailYears
    Residential electricity use, and each ZIP’s share of the summer peak (capacity tag)NYSERDA Utility Energy Registry (Con Edison)177 ZIP codes, monthly2024–2025
    Residential electricity use, San Diego CountySDG&E Energy Data Request Program86 ZIP codes, monthly2019
    Home size and share of 1–2 family homesNYC MapPLUTO 26v2By ZIP code2026
    Surface temperature, tree canopy, povertyNYC Health Dept. and Census, as in Part 242 neighborhoods2009–2017
    Monthly residential sales, customers and revenue by utilityU.S. Energy Information Administration, Form EIA-861MFive utilities2024–2025
    Distance from the coastCensus ZIP areas and Natural Earth coastlineZIP center to shore2010

    San Diego uses 2019. The utility’s files cover about 1.32 million households in 2019 and 2020, then far fewer from 2022 on, apparently because most customers moved to community power programs. I skipped 2020 because pandemic stay-at-home patterns changed household electricity use that year.

    4. Method

    Air conditioning is the main thing that changes between spring and summer, so the extra electricity a household uses in summer is a fair measure of cooling demand:

    cooling kWh = avg Jun–Aug kWh per account − avg Apr, May, Oct kWh per account

    Utilities report residential accounts, not households. Most homes have their own account, but some apartment buildings share one master meter, so apartment areas are partly undercounted (0.65 accounts per housing unit in mostly-apartment ZIP codes, against 0.84 in mostly-house ZIP codes). I report everything per residential account.

    For New York I also use Con Edison’s capacity tag, the utility’s allocation of the system’s summer peak to each customer group. It is closely tied to summer use (correlation 0.96), so it is not an independent measure of peak demand, and it does not capture strain on individual feeders or commercial load. I relate both measures to heat, canopy, poverty and housing with weighted regressions, then test random-forest and linear models on places they never saw in training.

    5. Results

    San Diego: the farther from the ocean, the bigger the summer bill

    New York: housing, not heat, sets the summer peak

    New York reverses the obvious expectation. The neighborhoods with the hottest surfaces in Part 2 add less summer power per account (correlation −0.67). Surface temperature here comes from a single 2009 satellite image and mostly reflects pavement and building density, not air temperature: the hottest surfaces are dense apartment districts with small units. The biggest summer demand comes from Staten Island and parts of Queens, where most homes are houses.

    Tree canopy’s link to the peak is fragile. Holding home size, housing type, surface heat and poverty constant, 10 more points of canopy go with 0.07 to 0.11 kW less of the peak allocation per account, depending on the model (all statistically significant). Without surface heat in the model the link disappears, and canopy is only measured for 42 neighborhoods. Treat it as a lead worth testing with finer canopy data, not a finding.

    Can GeoAI predict where the grid strains?

    Two lessons follow. First, tree-based models, the workhorse of many GeoAI tools, cannot predict beyond the range of conditions they were trained on; a hotter inland ZIP code looks to them like the hottest coastal one. A simple trend line extrapolates better. Second, a model can look accurate overall while failing whole districts: the New York model separated boroughs well but missed Staten Island’s houses badly. Anyone selling a citywide or nationwide heat-risk score should report how it does on places and conditions it was not trained on. These are plain machine-learning models on area-level data; the test, not the model, is the point.

    What the extra summer power costs

    Table 2. Extra cost of summer electricity per account, June to August, at each utility’s 2024 average residential price (Con Edison 35.66¢ and SDG&E 43.63¢ per kWh).
    AreaExtra kWh a monthExtra cost per summer
    New York, citywide187$200
    New York, mostly apartments171$183
    New York, mostly houses252$270
    San Diego County, all75$98
    San Diego, coast (under 5 km)32$42
    San Diego, 30 km+ inland203$266

    These are rough figures at each utility’s average annual price; Con Edison charges more in summer. Prices are 2024 averages for customers who buy power from the utility; customers of community power programs pay different supply rates, and San Diego’s usage is from 2019, so these are estimates, not bills.

    6. The largest cities

    For this study I used ZIP code data only for New York and San Diego, but the federal government publishes monthly totals for every large utility. That allows a city-to-city comparison of how much summer adds to each account’s use. The New York figure from this source, 192 extra kWh a month, is consistent with the 187 from Con Edison’s ZIP code data, though the two cover slightly different customers.

    Table 3. Summer demand and its rough cost by city, from federal monthly utility totals (so New York’s figures differ slightly from the ZIP code data above). Prices are each utility’s 2024 average residential price.
    City (utility)Summer vs. spring and fallExtra kWh a monthPriceExtra cost per summer
    Phoenix (APS and SRP)+86%79315.1¢$360
    Chicago (ComEd)+81%36815.2¢$168
    New York (Con Edison)+65%19235.7¢$206
    Los Angeles (LADWP)+7%3323.8¢$24
    HoustonNot available: Houston homes buy power from competing retailers, and the monthly federal data does not break out Houston.

    Phoenix households add four times as much summer electricity as New York households, but New York’s high prices mean its summer bill rises more than Chicago’s. Los Angeles barely changes, much like San Diego’s coast. These are utility-wide figures: ComEd and Arizona Public Service serve far beyond city limits, and Con Edison includes Westchester. San Diego is left out of this table because SDG&E’s recent totals cover only the households still buying power from the utility, about 285,000 of them.

    7. What it means

    For utilities: in New York, the summer peak per account is set mostly by the housing stock, so building records are a better guide to where load will grow than heat maps. In San Diego, distance from the coast is the first thing to look at.

    For cities: this study cannot show that trees lower summer demand; the canopy link was too sensitive to the model. Trees’ cooling and health benefits stand on other evidence.

    For anyone building GeoAI models: report how the model does on places it has never seen. In New York, models that looked accurate overall failed on whole boroughs; in San Diego, a tree-based model failed beyond the conditions it was trained on.

    For equity: low summer use in hot apartment neighborhoods is not good news on its own. It can mean smaller homes, but it can also mean households going without air conditioning. Part 2 found that heat illness tracked poverty, so lower demand in those areas should not be read as lower need. I did not measure air-conditioner ownership or master-metered buildings, so this study cannot separate small homes from missing air conditioning.

    8. Repeat it in ArcGIS Pro

    The same analysis in ArcGIS Pro, adapted from Esri’s published heat-risk workflow.

    1. Add the ESA WorldCover land-cover layer from ArcGIS Living Atlas and the ZIP code boundaries.
    2. Mark tree pixels with the Remap raster function (tree cover = 1, everything else = 0).
    3. Run Zonal Statistics as Table by ZIP code, then Calculate Field for percent canopy.
    4. Join the ZIP code electricity table and compute cooling kWh with Calculate Field.
    5. Find clusters of high summer demand with Hot Spot Analysis (Getis-Ord Gi*).
    6. Model demand with Generalized Linear Regression, then a forest-based model, holding out one area as validation.

    The Python code, the data, and a note on how each dataset was pulled will be on GitHub, like Part 2’s.

    9. Limits

    • Monthly totals measure summer demand, not the single hottest hour. Con Edison’s capacity tag is the closest measure of peak demand available here.
    • San Diego’s figures are from 2019. Recent SDG&E files cover only part of the customer base, and the 2026 heat waves are not in any published file yet.
    • New York’s canopy, surface heat and poverty are measured for 42 neighborhoods and shared by the ZIP codes inside them. The canopy estimates use statistical tests that account for that grouping.
    • Surface temperature (2009) and canopy (2014) are older than the electricity data.
    • Spring use is not zero cooling, especially in San Diego, so cooling demand is approximate.
    • San Diego’s comparison uses distance from the coast only. Housing and income for San Diego are not yet included.
    • The city comparison uses whole utility service areas, which do not match city limits.
    • San Diego relies on one year. ZIP-level summer increases in 2018 and 2019 agree only loosely (rank correlation 0.70), and some 2018 values are implausible, so I used 2019 alone.
    • Dollar figures use average annual prices; summer rates are often higher, and customers of energy service companies and community power programs pay different supply rates.
    • Results describe ZIP codes and neighborhoods, not individual households, and show association, not cause.

    Data and sources

    1. San Diego record demand, September 2026: reported by the San Diego Union-Tribune; outage figures from SDG&E; both summarized in The Cool Down.
    2. SDG&E (2024). Heat wave drives record electricity demand (5,032 MW, September 2024).
    3. San Diego October temperature records: Axios San Diego, citing National Weather Service records.
    4. Donovan, G. H., & Butry, D. R. (2009). The value of shade: Estimating the effect of urban trees on summertime electricity use. Energy and Buildings, 41(6), 662.
    5. 2006 Queens blackout: summary of events; state regulators’ January 2007 report called Con Edison’s performance “unacceptable and a gross disservice to its customers” (New York Sun).
    6. City of New York (2017). Cool Neighborhoods NYC.
    7. NYSERDA. Utility Energy Registry: Monthly ZIP Code Energy Use.
    8. SDG&E. Energy Data Request Program.
    9. NYC Department of City Planning. MapPLUTO 26v2, via NYC Open Data.
    10. U.S. Energy Information Administration. Form EIA-861M monthly sales to ultimate customers, 2024 and 2025 (2025 preliminary).
    11. U.S. Energy Information Administration. 2024 Utility Bundled Retail Sales, Residential (Form EIA-861).

      Community and equity research, UC San Diego, 2023

      Greater Logan Heights: Housing and Transportation

      A census-tract study of how decades of disinvestment in housing and transportation affected access to jobs, services and opportunity in one of San Diego's oldest Latino neighborhoods.

      About seven in ten homes have been rented since 2005

      Greater Logan Heights is in Southeastern San Diego, hemmed in by Interstates 5, 15 and 94. Decisions about infrastructure here have often been made without asking the people who live here. In April 1970, residents of Barrio Logan found out the city planned to put a Highway Patrol station under the Coronado Bridge. They occupied the land and got a park there instead, Chicano Park.

      The census numbers have barely moved. In the 2017-2021 data, 70.9% of occupied units in Greater Logan Heights were rented, compared with about 53% citywide, and the share has stayed near 70% since 2005-2009. Over the same years more workers drove to work, and fewer took transit, walked or biked.

      With the Logan Heights Community Development Corporation as our partner, we looked at how changes in housing and transportation have affected residents' access to jobs, services and opportunity, and what that means for daily life.

      Role
      Co-lead researcher and co-author (with Himig Reyes)
      When
      UC San Diego, 2023
      Team
      Jhoven (Johan) Fernandez and Himig Reyes (executive summary, introduction, methodology); Erliza Balaoing and Jackson Patten (literature review). Community partner: Logan Heights Community Development Corporation. Advising: Professor Mirle Rabinowitz Bussell and UGIA Jonathan Lalouz.
      Status
      Completed report
      Methods
      American Community Survey trend analysis (three 5-year periods), Census tract comparison against the City of San Diego, Literature review, Stakeholder interviews, Historical and government document review
      Tools and data
      ACS 5-year estimates (2005-2009, 2010-2014, 2017-2021), Census tract mapping

      The neighborhood and our question

      The Logan Heights Community Development Corporation defines Greater Logan Heights as five neighborhoods: Memorial, Stockton, Sherman Heights, Grant Hill and Logan Heights. The area has deep cultural roots and close community ties, but it hasn't shared in the region's growth.

      We wanted to know how changes in housing and transportation infrastructure have affected residents' access to jobs, services and other opportunities, and their daily lives. Our argument was that a long pattern of disinvestment in housing and transportation has hurt the community's physical, social and economic health.

      I wrote the introduction and co-wrote the executive summary and methodology with Himig Reyes. We worked with the Logan Heights CDC, which leads development efforts in the neighborhood.

      Earlier research on transit, housing and displacement

      Erliza Balaoing and Jackson Patten wrote our literature review, which covered housing disinvestment, transit access and displacement. Four findings from it guided how we read the data.

      • Transit and housing should be planned together. The Center for Transit-Oriented Development's 2014 guidebook for HUD shows that transportation is the second-largest household cost after housing, and that households in walkable places spend much less of their income getting around.
      • Transit investment in Latino neighborhoods can help residents or push them out. Gerardo Sandoval's national study of Latino immigrant neighborhoods, which included Logan Heights, found that outcomes were more equitable when residents guided the process and it built on the social, political and cultural assets already there.
      • Sidewalks are contested. Loukaitou-Sideris and Ehrenfeucht show that sidewalk rules and designs get negotiated between groups with unequal power, so planners need to ask who a street is being designed for.
      • Worries about crime near transit don't always hold up. Billings, Leland and Swindell found that Charlotte's light rail did not raise crime around stations, and property crime fell after station locations were announced.

      Data and methods

      We used American Community Survey 5-year estimates from 2005-2009, 2010-2014 and 2017-2021, so we could follow change over about fifteen years instead of looking at one point in time.

      We used census tracts 39.01, 39.02, 40, 47, 48 and 49 to stand for Greater Logan Heights. Tracts 41 and 46 include small parts of the northern neighborhood, but they also cover areas outside it, so we left them out to avoid skewing the results.

      We compared the tracts with each other to see differences inside the community, and compared the tracts combined with the City of San Diego. When the numbers needed context, we drew on interviews with people working on housing and transportation in the neighborhood, along with historical and government records.

      • Housing variables: median rent and home value, age of housing, tenure, units per structure, vacancy.
      • Transportation variables: means of transportation to work and travel time to work, for workers 16 and over.

      What the census data showed

      Most housing is rented, old and low-density. In the 2017-2021 data, 70.9% of occupied units were renter-occupied. Citywide the split was closer to even, with about 53% renters. The share here has stayed near 70% since 2005-2009, which means renters have had few chances to buy a home and build wealth that way.

      Costs differ a lot within the neighborhood. In 2021, median gross rent went from $1,264 in the lowest tract to $1,812 in the highest, while the citywide median was $1,611. Buildings are much older than the city average and often poorly maintained. Vacancy has been dropping but has generally stayed above the citywide rate.

      More people are driving. Driving to work went up from 2005 to 2021, with a jump in 2017-2021, while transit, walking and biking went down. We also found few comfortable bus stops, few PRONTO outlets for buying bus and trolley fares, and almost no dedicated bike lanes.

      In every period most workers had fairly short commutes. Trips over 40 minutes spiked in 2010-2014 and had dropped again by 2017-2021.

      • Recommendation 1: invest in fixing up existing homes, both for upkeep and for structural safety.
      • Recommendation 2: build more housing, at higher density, across the neighborhood.
      • Recommendation 3: allow property subdivision, which would make buying a home easier and give more people a way to build wealth.
      • Our project summary also called for new affordable housing, better transit options and better bike infrastructure.

      Limitations and next steps

      The ACS is based on samples. Margins of error for small tracts can be large, and hard-to-reach groups, including many minority residents, can be undercounted. Our most recent data was from 2021, two years before the report.

      We only used interviews here and there and didn't run a systematic survey, so the report relies more on census trends than on what residents told us. The recommendations are mostly about housing, and the transportation findings should get recommendations of their own.

      If I picked this up again, I would add the 2018-2022 and later ACS releases, map bus stop amenities and bike lanes directly, and do structured interviews with residents alongside the census work. I'd also want to check whether density can be added without the kind of displacement Sandoval warns about.

      Case studies

      • Barrio Logan, San Diego, CAChicano Park

        In April 1970 residents occupied land under the Coronado Bridge when they learned the city planned a Highway Patrol station there, and they got a park instead. I-5, the bridge and industrial rezoning had already split up the area. The park is now a National Historic Landmark.

        Lesson for this project: For decades, infrastructure decisions in this part of San Diego have been made without residents, and organized residents have changed the outcome before.

        Source
      • Oakland, CAFruitvale Transit Village

        When BART proposed a large commuter parking structure at Fruitvale station in 1991, the Unity Council, a local Latino community development corporation, objected and led a mixed-use village project instead. It has mixed-income housing, a clinic, a library, a senior center, shops and a plaza connecting the station to the main street.

        Lesson for this project: A neighborhood CDC like the Logan Heights CDC can turn a transit investment into housing and services for the people already living there.

        Source
      • Los Angeles, Oakland and San Diego, CAEquitable TOD in Latino immigrant neighborhoods

        Gerardo Sandoval studied MacArthur Park, Boyle Heights, Fruitvale and Logan Heights, and found that transit-oriented development can strengthen Latino neighborhoods when residents guide it. Examples include Boyle Heights' Mariachi Plaza and the Chicano Park muralists in Logan Heights.

        Lesson for this project: If our density recommendation went ahead, it would need community control and cultural placemaking from the start, or it could displace the residents it's meant to help.

        Source

      Sources

      2. Sandoval, G. (2017). Developing a Model for Transit-Oriented Development in Latino Immigrant Communities (project brief). National Institute for Transportation and Communities. Link

      Community and equity research, USP 138, UC San Diego

      City Heights: People and Needs

      A needs assessment of City Heights in San Diego. It focuses on high school graduation and also proposes programs for senior care and culture.

      Both City Heights high schools graduate fewer students than the city average

      City Heights is a young neighborhood. In the 2020 Census its median age was 31.7, compared with 36.3 for San Diego County. It has 76,624 residents, including many immigrant and refugee families, and about 63% of residents speak a language other than English at home.

      San Diego's average graduation rate was 91%. Hoover High graduated 83% and Crawford High 85%. Among adults in the neighborhood, about 42% had less than a high school diploma. Research on dropping out finds that it happens gradually, with warning signs along the way.

      With Joshua Lee and Jaehee Nam, I looked at what high school students in City Heights need, and how meeting those needs could improve their grades and their options later on.

      Role
      Team member (with Joshua Lee and Jaehee Nam)
      When
      USP 138, UC San Diego
      Team
      Joshua Lee, Jaehee Nam and Jhoven (Johan) Fernandez, for USP 138 (Anderson).
      Status
      Completed report
      Methods
      Demographic profile from census and forecast data, School performance comparison, Literature and policy review, Program proposals
      Tools and data
      2020 U.S. Census, U.S. Census Bureau time series, U.S. News & World Report high school data

      Research question

      What are the educational needs and challenges of high school students in City Heights, San Diego, and how could they be addressed to improve academic outcomes and future opportunities?

      City Heights is one of San Diego's youngest and most diverse neighborhoods, with many immigrant and refugee families. Joshua Lee, Jaehee Nam and I started the needs assessment with who lives there, then moved on to what the neighborhood is missing.

      Education was the main need we focused on. We also looked at seniors' medical needs and at cultural needs, since they affect the same households.

      Why we started with high school completion

      Two outside studies helped explain why high school completion was a good place to start.

      • Students usually drop out gradually. Russell Rumberger, director of the California Dropout Research Project, has argued that there are warning signs along the way, and that failing in middle and high school is the best predictor.
      • Neighborhood programs and school quality have different effects. Dobbie and Fryer's lottery study of the Harlem Children's Zone Promise Academy found large math gains, and the evidence suggested they came from the school itself and much less from the community programs around it.

      Data and methods

      We put together a demographic profile from the 2020 Census, Census Bureau trends and a 2025 ethnicity forecast. We compared the two City Heights high schools with the San Diego average on graduation rates, enrollment and college readiness scores, and used published research on the costs of dropping out.

      For each need, we proposed programs aimed at the specific gap we found.

      Findings and proposals

      City Heights had 76,624 residents in the 2020 Census, with 3.04 persons per household. The median age was 31.7, compared with 36.3 for San Diego County. About 63% of residents speak a language other than English at home, mostly Spanish and Vietnamese. The 2025 forecast put the population at about 52% Hispanic, 18% Asian, 15% white and 11% Black.

      Education levels were low. About 42% of adults had less than a high school diploma, and only 15% had a bachelor's degree or higher.

      San Diego's average graduation rate was 91%. Hoover High (2,147 students in grades 9-12) graduated 83% and Crawford High (1,117 students) graduated 85%. College readiness scores were 33.7 at Hoover and 27.4 at Crawford, compared with a city average of about 38.

      Seniors went from 5.8% of residents in 2000 to 9.7% in 2019, so there is more need for primary care, home health, transportation, and services in residents' own languages and cultures. We also noted that immigrant families often lose fluency in their native language by the third generation.

      • Education proposals: an English language program for all ages, after-school tutoring, and a recreation program for high schoolers who are falling behind or cut off from their peers.
      • Cultural proposals: weekend language schools with proficiency tests that could count for college credit; night markets featuring Vietnamese, Somali, Cambodian, Laotian and Latino cultures, with entry fees paying for the language schools; guest speakers in high schools; recognition of holidays such as Tet, Eid al-Fitr and Day of the Dead; and a museum of the neighborhood's ethnic communities.

      Limitations and next steps

      This was a desk study. We didn't survey or interview students, families or teachers, so the needs come from data and not from talking to people. The graduation rates and readiness scores are one year's numbers for two schools.

      We didn't estimate costs for the proposals or compare them with programs already running in the neighborhood, and City Heights already has strong education partnerships.

      Next, I would map where students live in relation to their schools and after-school options, interview students and counselors at Hoover and Crawford, and compare each proposal with what local partners already offer before suggesting anything new.

      Case studies

      • City Heights, San Diego, CACity Heights Educational Collaborative

        Since 1998, San Diego State University, San Diego Unified, the teachers' association and Price Charities have partnered with Rosa Parks Elementary, Monroe Clark Middle and Hoover High. The College Avenue Compact (2007) guaranteed SDSU admission to qualifying students. Hoover graduates enrolling at SDSU went from 20 in fall 2005 to 57 planned for fall 2009.

        Lesson for this project: New programs in City Heights should build on this K-12 to college pipeline instead of duplicating it.

        Source
      • New York, NYHarlem Children's Zone Promise Academy

        A lottery-based evaluation by Dobbie and Fryer found Promise Academy middle school students scored 0.28 standard deviations higher in math than students who lost the lottery. The gains seemed to come from the school more than from the neighborhood programs.

        Lesson for this project: Tutoring and recreation are still worth doing, but the biggest gains may depend on what happens inside Hoover and Crawford.

        Source

      Sources

      1. San Diego State University (2009). City Heights collaborative creates college-going atmosphere. SDSU News. Link
      2. Dobbie, W., and Fryer, R. High-Quality Schools and Achievement Among the Poor in the United States. J-PAL evaluation summary. Link
      3. Alliance for Excellent Education (2008). Straight A's: Public Education Policy and Progress, 8(17), reporting Russell Rumberger, California Dropout Research Project. Link

      Community and equity research, UC San Diego, 2023

      Revelle Plaza: Green Space and Student Well-Being

      A mixed-methods study of how students use and rate one of UC San Diego's oldest open spaces, plus a plan for scaling the study up to a campus-wide green space redesign.

      A lot of campus open space goes unused

      Revelle Plaza is at the center of UC San Diego's first college and is one of the oldest open spaces on campus. Universities have a lot of space like this, and much of it sits empty when there's nothing for students to do there.

      This affects more than how a campus looks. In Auckland, more usable green space within 3 km was associated with lower treatment rates for anxiety and mood disorders. In Wisconsin, a study of 2,479 residents linked more neighborhood green space to fewer symptoms of depression, anxiety and stress. In New York, William H. Whyte found that seating, sun, food and other people determine where crowds gather.

      We went to the plaza and counted students by zone in three time periods, surveyed them and did short interviews. The pilot looks at how a green space's design and layout affect whether students use it and how they feel there.

      Role
      Researcher (with Ethan Lee and Karina Wong)
      When
      UC San Diego, 2023
      Team
      Ethan Lee and Karina Wong. Advisor: Professor Amy Lerner.
      Status
      Pilot
      Methods
      Observational counts across three time periods, Student surveys (open-ended), Short structured interviews, Literature review
      Tools and data
      Behavioral mapping of key plaza zones, Survey and interview instruments

      Research question

      Revelle Plaza seemed like a good place to start, since it's one of the oldest open spaces on campus and sits at the center of UC San Diego's first college.

      We asked how the design and layout of green space affect whether students use it and how they feel there, and which design changes could get more students using it and enjoying it. Revelle Plaza was our test case.

      I did the study with Ethan Lee and Karina Wong, with guidance from Professor Amy Lerner.

      Research on green space and mental health

      The study builds on a well-established link between green space and mental health, and on a smaller body of work about why some plazas get used and others don't.

      • Access to green space is linked to better mental health. Nutsford, Pearson and Kingham (2013) found in Auckland that more usable green space within 3 km, and a shorter distance to the nearest one, were associated with lower treatment rates for anxiety and mood disorders.
      • The link also shows up at the neighborhood level. Beyer and colleagues (2014) studied 2,479 Wisconsin residents and found that more neighborhood green space went with fewer symptoms of depression, anxiety and stress.
      • Nature helps people recover from mental fatigue. Stephen Kaplan's attention restoration framework (1995) explains why time in natural settings can restore the focus that studying and work use up, which is relevant on a campus.
      • Design details affect use. William H. Whyte's observations of New York plazas showed that people are drawn most by other people, and that seating, sun and food affect where they gather.

      How we studied the plaza

      We combined counts, interviews and surveys so we could compare what students did with what they said.

      We counted students in several key areas of the plaza during three time periods to see which zones attracted people and when. The short interviews asked a set of yes/no questions and ended by asking what students would improve. The surveys asked open-ended questions about students' experiences and habits in the plaza.

      • Observation: total counts by plaza zone, three time periods.
      • Interviews: yes/no items plus one open question about improvements.
      • Surveys: open-ended questions on experience and behavior.

      Results so far and a proposed larger study

      The pilot gave us a field method for studying one plaza: where students cluster, when the space empties out, and what they say is missing. I haven't yet written up the detailed counts and response themes in a form I can publish here.

      Based on the pilot, I drafted a plan to study the same question across the campus. Everything below is a plan with target numbers. None of it is a result.

      • Proposed: a literature review of 50 or more scholarly articles on green space design and student well-being.
      • Proposed: an online survey of 1,200 students and 15 focus groups, analyzed with statistics and thematic coding.
      • Proposed: a redesign of about 10,000 square feet of campus space into distinct zones for quiet study, physical activity and social time, developed with landscape architects, students, faculty and campus facilities.
      • Proposed: a post-implementation survey and focus groups with 800 students.
      • Target outcomes set in the proposal: a 35% increase in green space use and a 25% improvement in student-reported well-being. These are targets we would test. They aren't findings.

      Limitations and next steps

      The pilot covered one plaza during a few time periods, with a convenience sample of students. It can show how the space is used, but it can't prove that design changes well-being.

      The proposal lists its own obstacles: getting a representative mix of students, the physical limits of existing spaces, administrative approval and cost.

      Next, I would publish the pilot counts and survey themes. Before trying a 10,000 square foot redesign, I'd run a before-and-after comparison around a small change, such as movable seating or shade. Adding a comparison plaza that stays the same would make the result much more convincing.

      Case studies

      • New York, NYBryant Park restoration

        Bryant Park used to be avoided and was overrun by drug dealing. Starting in the 1980s it was redesigned on William H. Whyte's advice. The park was lowered toward street level, hedges and fences came out, more entrances were added, and thousands of movable chairs were brought in. It now gets about 25,000 visitors a day in warm months.

        Lesson for this project: Small, cheap changes like clearer sightlines, more entrances and movable seating can change how a plaza is used without rebuilding it.

        Source
      • New York, NYStreet Life Project

        Starting in 1969, Whyte and his assistants used time-lapse film and direct observation to record how people actually used plazas and streets, and published the results as The Social Life of Small Urban Spaces (1980). The Project for Public Spaces grew out of this method.

        Lesson for this project: Counting people by zone and time of day, which is what we did at Revelle, is a well-tested way to assess a public space before redesigning it.

        Source

      Sources

      1. Nutsford, D., Pearson, A. L., and Kingham, S. (2013). An ecological study investigating the association between access to urban green space and mental health. Public Health, 127(11), 1005-1011. Link
      2. Beyer, K. M. M., Kaltenbach, A., Szabo, A., Bogar, S., Nieto, F. J., and Malecki, K. M. (2014). Exposure to neighborhood green space and mental health: evidence from the Survey of the Health of Wisconsin. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health, 11(3), 3453-3472. Link
      3. Kaplan, S. (1995). The restorative benefits of nature: toward an integrative framework. Journal of Environmental Psychology, 15(3), 169-182. Link
      4. Project for Public Spaces. William H. Whyte. Link
      5. American Planning Association (2010). Bryant Park, New York, New York. Great Places in America. Link

      GIS and spatial technology, UC San Diego Facilities Management, Feb 2023 to Mar 2024

      Georeferencing CAD Files for UC San Diego Campus Buildings

      Putting 1,788 campus building drawings on the map, with world files and a QA checklist, so UC San Diego's facilities data could share one coordinate system.

      Campus floor plans had no real-world coordinates

      UC San Diego keeps floor plans for buildings on the La Jolla East and West campuses, at Scripps Institution of Oceanography and at UC San Diego Health. Each drawing was accurate internally, but each used its own local coordinates. There was no way to line up a room in one file with a street, a utility line or a building in another.

      This has practical effects. Deciding which buildings get maintenance, which rooms get reassigned and where new work goes depends on data that people trust and can line up. A drawing with no location can't be part of that.

      From February 2023 to March 2024, Kushinga Pfende and I worked through 1,788 of these files, one control point at a time. We wanted to tie all the campus buildings to the campus GIS in a way someone else could check, repeat and build on.

      Role
      GIS Project Assistant (with Kushinga Pfende)
      When
      UC San Diego Facilities Management, Feb 2023 to Mar 2024
      Team
      Kushinga Pfende (GIS student collaborator), Diana Henderson (project supervisor), Sung Lee (GIS Analyst, CAD library and control points)
      Status
      Completed
      Methods
      Control-point georeferencing, World file creation, Spreadsheet-based QA/QC checklist, Multi-campus data integration
      Tools and data
      ArcGIS, CAD floor plan library, Campus GIS spatial database, Facilities spreadsheet

      The problem

      UC San Diego has a large library of CAD drawings: floor plans and layouts for buildings on the La Jolla East and West campuses, Scripps Institution of Oceanography, UC San Diego Health and other sites. Each drawing was accurate internally but used its own local coordinates, so a room in one file couldn't be lined up with a street, a utility line or a building in another.

      We wanted to give every drawing real-world coordinates so all the buildings could be viewed, measured and queried with the rest of the campus GIS.

      We also wanted to do it in a way that someone else could check, repeat and build on, because decisions about maintenance, room assignments and new work depend on data people trust and can line up.

      Background: Esri's CAD workflow and campus digital twins

      We followed Esri's documented workflow for CAD data. You assign a spatial reference first, then move, rotate and scale the drawing into place, using control points that match features in the drawing to the same features on the map. The result is saved to a world file that ArcGIS reads every time the drawing loads.

      Other researchers describe this kind of work as a first step toward a campus digital twin. Meschini and colleagues (2022) built a BIM-GIS asset management system for the University of Turin, which has buildings at many sites. They found that georeferencing all of the buildings was what allowed scattered departmental records to be combined into one relational database.

      • Esri: control points define the transformation, and a spatial reference is required for it to be accurate.
      • Esri: a CAD world file stores point pairs describing a 2D transformation and needs a matching .prj file for the coordinate system.
      • Esri also notes that the best CAD-GIS workflows skip world files altogether by drawing in geospatial coordinates from the start.
      • Meschini et al. (2022): georeferenced buildings are the base layer for a digital twin of a university with many sites.

      How we did it

      Kushinga Pfende and I worked from the CAD library that Facilities keeps on OneDrive. Sung Lee helped put together the library and the control points. Diana Henderson supervised the project and guided the methodology and ArcGIS workflow.

      We brought the drawings into ArcGIS and converted them to a geodatabase format. For each drawing, we matched recognizable features (survey markers, road intersections, sidewalks and other landmarks) to their known locations in the campus GIS spatial database. These control points determine where the drawing sits, how it's rotated and how it's scaled.

      I also made a georeferencing checklist from a facilities spreadsheet the university gave us. It already had facility number, name, total floors, floor plan IDs and area. I added columns for georeferencing status, comments and a needs-review flag, and then went through every row.

      • For buildings with more than one floor, I checked that the floor plan IDs matched the listed number of floors.
      • For each building, I recorded the coordinate system, units, origin coordinates, scale and rotation angle from the world file parameters.
      • After every file was georeferenced, I filtered for rows flagged for another review, which gave us a clear list of files to adjust.

      What we produced

      The main deliverable was 1,788 georeferenced CAD files, each with a world file holding its coordinate information. Building drawings from all of UC San Diego's campuses could now be laid over the campus basemap and analyzed with other GIS layers.

      The checklist turned into a quality assurance tool. It shows which buildings still need adjusting before they line up with the campus basemap at survey grade, and it was set up so it could guide and check CAD mapping for new campus projects.

      Together, these give Facilities one coordinate system for classrooms, offices and other assets. That's what asset tracking, measurement and 3D visualization for a campus digital twin would need to start from.

      Limitations and next steps

      World files work around the underlying problem. Every new or revised drawing made in local coordinates will need the same treatment, which is why Esri recommends drawing in real coordinates from the start. A good next step would be a CAD standard for new campus projects that requires a known coordinate system.

      We didn't record a formal accuracy measure in the checklist, such as residual error per control point. With one, the needs-review flag could be based on a threshold instead of judgment, and the survey-grade goal could actually be tested.

      Georeferenced drawings are also still just drawings. Turning them into structured features (rooms, uses, occupants) would make it possible to answer questions about how space is shared across departments and campuses.

      Case studies

      • Turin, ItalyUniversity of Turin BIM-GIS asset management

        Researchers georeferenced all of the university's buildings, which are spread across many locations, and linked BIM models into a GIS-based web platform with dashboards and a single relational database.

        Lesson for this project: Georeferencing every building is what allows separate departmental records to be combined into one campus-wide asset system.

        Source
      • Seattle, WashingtonUniversity of Washington automated indoor mapping

        UW Facilities built automated FME workflows that convert AutoCAD floor plans into a geodatabase on a schedule, covering about 1,700 floors and 24 million square feet of interior space.

        Lesson for this project: After the drawings are georeferenced, automating the CAD-to-GIS update keeps the campus map up to date without redoing the manual work.

        Source
      • Amherst, MassachusettsUMass Amherst indoor asset mapping

        UMass Amherst moved its asset inventory indoors using georeferenced CAD floor plans and 360-degree photos in ArcGIS Pro, and hoped to build a pedestrian accessibility network later on.

        Lesson for this project: Georeferenced floor plans make it possible to ask indoor questions, such as about accessibility, that outdoor maps can't answer.

        Source

      Sources

      1. Esri. Georeference CAD data. ArcGIS Pro 3.5 documentation. Link
      2. Esri. World files for CAD and BIM data. ArcGIS Pro 3.2 documentation. Link
      3. Meschini, S., Pellegrini, L., Locatelli, M., Accardo, D., Tagliabue, L. C., Di Giuda, G. M., and Avena, M. (2022). Toward cognitive digital twins using a BIM-GIS asset management system for a diffused university. Frontiers in Built Environment, 8. Link
      4. Safe Software. The University of Washington automates indoor mapping process. Customer story. Link
      5. Wrenner, R., and Okscin, A. (2018). Facilities track: Mapping a university inside and out. NEARC Fall 2018. Link

      GIS and spatial technology, UC San Diego Facilities Management, Sep 2023 to Mar 2024

      UC San Diego Drone Flight Initiative

      Setting up a drone-mapping workflow for campus planning that follows the rules, from DJI Mavic 3 Enterprise flights to orthomosaics and 3D terrain models in ArcGIS.

      Using drones to get current imagery of campus sites

      If you want to know what a UC San Diego building site looks like today, the basemap may show you imagery that is months or years old. Satellite and aerial imagery is often too coarse for site work, and walking the site and taking notes is slow and hard to compare over time.

      Drones can help, but flying is only part of the job. Under FAA Part 107, pilots need a remote pilot certificate, flights have to stay below 400 feet and in visual line of sight, and flying in controlled airspace requires authorization. Accuracy depends a lot on where the ground control points go, as well as on the software. After all that, the imagery still has to get into the GIS that Facilities already uses.

      From September 2023 to March 2024, I led a pilot with DJI Mavic 3 Enterprise drones across UC San Diego's colleges. We wanted to see if a small team could fly safely and legally, turn the imagery into accurate products, and get those products to campus planners.

      Role
      GIS Project Assistant, initiative lead
      When
      UC San Diego Facilities Management, Sep 2023 to Mar 2024
      Status
      Pilot
      Methods
      UAS flight planning and operations, Photogrammetry, Orthomosaic and 3D terrain model production, Equipment evaluation, Regulatory compliance review
      Tools and data
      DJI Mavic 3 Enterprise, ArcGIS Drone2Map, Pix4D, Agisoft Metashape, ArcGIS Online

      The problem

      Campus planners at UC San Diego need up-to-date imagery showing what was built, what changed and what needs attention. Satellite and aerial basemaps are often months or years old and too coarse for site work, and site walks are slow and hard to compare over time.

      I led a campus-wide initiative to test whether drones could help with infrastructure planning, environmental monitoring and sustainability analysis. Specifically, could a small team fly safely and legally, turn the imagery into accurate products, and get them into the GIS that Facilities already uses?

      To answer that, we had to look at more than the drone. Flight rules, camera settings, processing choices and data storage all affect whether an image ends up being useful to a planner.

      Background: ground control points and FAA rules

      Drone photogrammetry turns overlapping photos into orthomosaics, point clouds and terrain models. Their accuracy depends heavily on ground control points (GCPs), which are marked locations measured separately on the ground. Ferrer-González and colleagues (2020) tested different numbers and layouts of GCPs and found that placement matters as much as quantity. Points alternating between the two sides of a corridor did better than other layouts with the same number of points or more.

      Flying on a campus is also regulated. Under the FAA's Part 107 rules, commercial and institutional pilots need a remote pilot certificate, registered aircraft that broadcast Remote ID, flights below 400 feet with the drone in visual line of sight, and airspace authorization (for example through LAANC) in controlled airspace. Night flights, flights over people and flights beyond line of sight need waivers.

      Some universities now manage drones as a shared service instead of as one-off projects. In March 2026 the University of Arizona launched an Integrated Aerial Operations program that sends every campus drone flight request through one coordination center. It covers facilities inspections, parking analysis and geospatial mapping under FAA rules and university policy.

      • Accuracy depends on how GCPs are laid out in the field, as well as on the software.
      • Following the rules has to be built into the workflow from the start. Airspace, people on the ground and pilot certification all limit where and when you can fly.

      How I did it

      I used DJI Mavic 3 Enterprise drones to capture high-resolution imagery across UC San Diego's colleges. I planned every flight to meet FAA Part 107 and UC San Diego Environment, Health and Safety (EH&S) requirements.

      I processed the imagery in ArcGIS Drone2Map and Pix4D, also had Agisoft Metashape available, and published the results through ArcGIS Online. Using more than one processing package let me compare how each one handled the same campus data.

      The initiative had four objectives. We wanted to set up a full drone-mapping workflow for campus planning, bring aerial data into GIS asset-management systems, keep every flight within FAA and EH&S rules, and give people hands-on training in photogrammetry and flight operations.

      Training was planned in from the beginning. I wanted a workflow that other people in Facilities could learn, repeat and check, from flight planning through processing and publishing, so the program wouldn't depend on one pilot.

      What came out of it

      We produced orthomosaic basemaps and 3D terrain models for campus planners and sustainability teams. By the project's own estimate, site inspections became more than 60 percent more efficient.

      I made a Drone Model Comparison Matrix to help with equipment purchases, so future buying decisions could be based on documented tradeoffs instead of brand familiarity.

      I also proposed a Drone Data Hub for UC San Diego Facilities Management and the RMP divisions. It's still only a proposal. The idea is a shared place where flights, imagery and the products made from them can be found and reused, instead of sitting on individual drives.

      • Orthomosaic basemaps for planners
      • 3D terrain models for sustainability teams
      • Drone Model Comparison Matrix
      • Proposed Drone Data Hub

      Limitations and next steps

      The 60 percent efficiency figure is the project's own estimate. Before relying on it, I'd want to document the baseline and how it was measured. Accuracy needs the same treatment. A formal check against surveyed checkpoints would show whether the orthomosaics are good enough for design work or only for planning.

      Several next steps are planned but haven't been done yet: vegetation and stormwater monitoring with multispectral sensors, change detection for construction and sustainability reporting, and AI-based feature extraction to build an infrastructure inventory.

      Drones also raise questions that technology can't settle. Who appears in the imagery, how long it's kept and who can see it are governance decisions, and a Drone Data Hub would be a good place to write those rules down.

      Case studies

      • Amherst, MassachusettsUMass Amherst campus UAS mapping

        In 2023 a UMass team mapped the 2.5-square-mile campus in blocks of roughly 600 m by 600 m with DJI Mavic drones. In the core campus they used RTK-surveyed ground control points every 200 to 300 meters, and produced orthomosaics and point clouds for coordinating construction.

        Lesson for this project: A campus-wide program needs a planned GCP layout, and that's the most obvious thing a UC San Diego follow-up should add.

        Source
      • MinnesotaMnDOT drone bridge inspections

        The Minnesota Department of Transportation used drones on 39 bridges in 2015 and 2016 instead of under-bridge vehicles, rope access and scaffolding. Costs dropped 40 percent on average, and the deliverables were better even where costs didn't drop.

        Lesson for this project: Claims about inspection efficiency are most convincing when they're compared against a specific baseline method and cost. This project's efficiency figure should be held to that standard.

        Source
      • Chula Vista, CaliforniaChula Vista Police drone as first responder

        Starting in October 2018 under the FAA's UAS Integration Pilot Program, Chula Vista police sent drones from headquarters to emergency calls. They flew within visual line of sight and under an FAA waiver for flights over people.

        Lesson for this project: This San Diego County program shows that expanding drone use takes work with the FAA on waivers and clear operating rules. A campus Drone Data Hub would need the same.

        Source

      Sources

      1. Ferrer-González, E., Agüera-Vega, F., Carvajal-Ramírez, F., and Martínez-Carricondo, P. (2020). UAV photogrammetry accuracy assessment for corridor mapping based on the number and distribution of ground control points. Remote Sensing. Link
      2. Federal Aviation Administration. Certified Remote Pilots including Commercial Operators (Part 107). Link
      3. University of Arizona (2026). Integrated Aerial Operations program centralizes unmanned aircraft systems (UAS) operations. UANews. Link
      4. UMass Amherst Trimble Technology Lab (2023). Mapping the UMass Amherst campus using UAS aerial imagery. Link
