      GIS and spatial technology, UC San Diego

      ArcGIS Indoors Pilot for UC San Diego

      Converting existing CAD floor plans into an Indoors dataset that knows which floor things are on, then using field forms to map safety equipment inside campus buildings.

      Campus maps usually don't cover building interiors

      Most campus maps don't show anything inside the buildings. Information you'd need in an emergency, like where the safety equipment is and how the floors connect, is usually in paper plans, PDFs or someone's memory.

      Emergency response researchers point out the same gap: GIS works well for dispatch outdoors, but indoor navigation is still underdeveloped. Mahdaviparsa and McCuen worked with a fire marshal's team to see which indoor maps first responders could read under pressure.

      UC San Diego already had a good starting point in its CAD floor plans, which show walls, doors and rooms in detail. I hadn't used ArcGIS Indoors before and learned it through the Esri Training Academy. In this pilot I tried to turn those plans into an indoor map organized by floor, with safety equipment collected in the field and shown in a viewer people could actually use.

      Role
      Pilot developer (data model, field forms, viewer configuration)
      When
      UC San Diego
      Status
      Pilot
      Methods
      CAD-to-Indoors data conversion, Field data collection with survey forms, Indoor web viewer configuration, Self-directed technical training
      Tools and data
      ArcGIS Pro (Indoors toolbox), ArcGIS Field Maps, ArcGIS Indoors Viewer, CAD floor plans

      The question

      Inside a building, the information that matters in an emergency is usually in paper plans, PDFs or someone's memory.

      I wanted to know whether UC San Diego's existing CAD floor plans could be turned into a working indoor map. Could I build a dataset organized by floor from those plans, collect the locations of safety equipment inside selected buildings, and show the result in a viewer people could use?

      The CAD floor plans made sense as a starting point. The university already maintains them, they show walls, doors and rooms in detail, and they can be reused without redrawing anything.

      Background: the Indoors data model and emergency response

      ArcGIS Indoors uses a published information model. It organizes indoor space as a hierarchy of sites, facilities (building footprints), levels (floors), units (rooms and other spaces) and details (walls, doors and windows), with optional pathways and transitions for routing between rooms and floors. Esri provides tools for importing CAD floor plans directly into that schema.

      Indoor maps are most useful when people can't see where they're going. Mahdaviparsa and McCuen (2019) compared ways of building indoor networks from BIM and CAD data for emergency response, and worked with a fire marshal's team to see which ones first responders could read under pressure. They start from the same gap this pilot was aimed at.

      Universities that use Indoors across their campuses describe a similar process. The University of Rhode Island moved its floor plans from a proprietary facility management system to CAD standards and then into the Indoors model. Its public safety staff now use those floor plans for emergency management and event coordination.

      • Because the data model is shared, a pilot built on a few buildings can be expanded to a whole campus without starting over.
      • For safety uses, the data has to be complete and also easy to read when people are under stress.

      How I built it

      I imported existing CAD floor plans into an Indoors dataset that I created with the Indoors toolbox in ArcGIS Pro. That gave me the layered structure the Indoors model expects, with levels, units, details and facility features.

      Next I created and managed survey forms in ArcGIS Field Maps and used them to record where safety equipment was inside the selected buildings. Collecting the points inside the building meant each one was tied to the correct floor and room, which is more reliable than guessing from a drawing.

      Near the end of the project I tried configuring the ArcGIS Indoors Viewer for our campus data, so people could browse the floor plans and collected points one floor at a time.

      Each step depended on the one before. Clean floor plans made the levels and units usable as a base map in Field Maps, and accurate field points gave the viewer something worth looking at.

      What came out of it

      The pilot produced a working Indoors dataset built from campus CAD plans, a set of Field Maps survey forms for collecting safety equipment, the safety equipment locations we collected in the selected buildings, and a first configuration of the Indoors Viewer.

      I also learned a lot. I hadn't used ArcGIS Indoors before this project, and all my training came from the Esri Training Academy and Esri's video documentation.

      It took a lot of trial and error. Many of my early attempts used data outside our area of interest, and narrowing the scope was part of figuring out how the Indoors model and its tools work.

      Limitations and next steps

      This was a pilot, and the viewer setup was experimental. It covered a few selected buildings and didn't include routing or occupant data.

      The scoping problems I ran into early on taught me to define the area of interest and the list of safety equipment before importing anything. A short data dictionary agreed on with campus safety staff would keep the field forms consistent and make the data easier to maintain.

      Next, I would test the viewer with the people who would use it in an emergency, as Mahdaviparsa and McCuen did with fire service staff, and set up a routine for updating the indoor data when floor plans or equipment change.

      Safety data inside buildings also raises questions about access. Who can see where equipment is, and whether the map should be public, internal or shared only with responders, is a policy decision the campus would need to make before going further.

      Case studies

      • Rhode IslandUniversity of Rhode Island smart campus

        URI started an ArcGIS Indoors pilot in 2022. It moved floor plans from an old facility management system to CAD standards and then to the Indoors model, and now uses Indoors floor plans for public safety, emergency management and event coordination.

        Lesson for this project: A pilot like mine can become a campus-wide safety and operations tool once the floor plans are standardized and someone is responsible for it.

        Source
      • New Jersey (Rutgers University)Rutgers Lucy Stone Hall indoor map

        A Rutgers geography student converted the CAD floor plans for a famously confusing building into ArcGIS layers with rooms, doors, stairwells and elevators. The student added turn-by-turn directions and presented it to campus planning and operations as a proof of concept in 2023.

        Lesson for this project: A small, clearly scoped student pilot can be enough to show campus decision makers what indoor GIS can do.

        Source

      Sources

      1. Esri. ArcGIS Indoors Information Model. ArcGIS Pro 3.4 documentation. Link
      2. Mahdaviparsa, A., and McCuen, T. (2019). Comparison between current methods of indoor network analysis for emergency response through BIM/CAD-GIS integration. In Advances in Informatics and Computing in Civil and Construction Engineering. Springer. Link
      3. Esri ArcUser. Empowering a university with smart campus GIS solutions (University of Rhode Island). Link
      4. Esri ArcWatch. ArcGIS demystifies a baffling building (Rutgers University). Link

      GIS and spatial technology, Action Research, Nov 2024 to Apr 2026

      Stormwater Planning and Compliance

      Work with Orange County cities on California's MS4 stormwater permit: shared workflows, GIS dashboards, outreach campaigns, and a regional study of how utility vault pump-outs get reported.

      Coordinating stormwater programs across four cities

      When it rains in Southern California, runoff picks up pesticides, oil and trash from streets and yards and carries them through storm drains into creeks and the ocean. Most of it doesn't come from any one pipe. It comes from everyday behavior on thousands of properties.

      So meeting the permit takes a lot of coordination. The San Diego Region's MS4 permit by itself covers 39 agencies. It's also hard to show that outreach works. A 2022 Washington State University synthesis found that only 13 percent of studies on stormwater behavior change campaigns used a control group.

      At Action Research I worked with four Orange County municipalities on dashboards, templates and outreach campaigns. The underlying question was how several agencies can run stormwater programs that fit together, report progress clearly and actually change what residents and businesses do.

      Role
      Project & Program Associate, Action Research
      When
      Action Research, Nov 2024 to Apr 2026
      Status
      Completed
      Methods
      Multi-jurisdictional program coordination, GIS dashboards and project tracking, Outreach campaign design and evaluation, Inter-agency interviews, Process assessment and recommendations
      Tools and data
      ArcGIS Online, Power BI, Excel, Smartsheet, Adobe Creative Suite, Microsoft Teams

      The problem

      Cities and counties are responsible for reducing runoff pollution under California's Municipal Separate Storm Sewer System (MS4) permits.

      Because most of the pollution comes from everyday behavior on thousands of properties, compliance depends on coordination and outreach as much as on pipes. At Action Research I led projects involving several jurisdictions, all working on the same basic problem: getting agencies' stormwater programs to fit together, report progress clearly and change what residents and businesses do.

      Background: permits and evidence on outreach

      Under the Clean Water Act's NPDES program, the EPA requires operators of municipal separate storm sewer systems to hold permits and run stormwater management programs, with public education and outreach as one required element. In California, Regional Water Boards issue these permits. Orange County is split between two regions: the Santa Ana Region permit for north and central Orange County, and the San Diego Region's regional MS4 permit (Order R9-2013-0001, as amended), which covers 39 agencies across San Diego County and parts of Orange and Riverside counties and requires Water Quality Improvement Plans for each watershed.

      The EPA calls nonpoint source pollution (runoff from lawns, streets and homes) the leading remaining cause of water quality problems. Since it comes from so many sources, outreach is one of the main tools, but it's hard to prove that outreach has an effect. A 2022 Washington State University synthesis of stormwater behavior change campaigns found that about 57 percent of studies with baseline data reported that people adopted the target behavior, while only 13 percent used a control group.

      • Permits set the requirements, but the work is spread across many cities with different staff and systems.
      • Outreach seems to work best when it targets one concrete behavior, such as pesticide use, and measures that behavior directly instead of only measuring awareness.

      What I did

      I worked with planners, engineers and communications specialists to help city and county agencies across Orange County carry out their MS4 programs. My part was connecting regulatory data to planning tools that staff could use.

      I coordinated planning and compliance workflows across four municipalities so that community outreach matched each city's local planning goals. I built GIS dashboards and project tracking systems that put site activities, compliance metrics and public participation results in one place.

      I also set up standard project governance templates to improve QA/QC, communication between departments and contract reporting. For outreach, I helped design and evaluate campaigns including Good, Bad and Bugly, HOA binder updates and pesticide reduction efforts.

      The TO39 study of vault pump-out reporting

      For the County of San Diego's Watershed Protection Department, I did a regional assessment of how utility vault pump-outs are reported. When utilities pump water out of underground vaults, it can go into the storm drain system, and inconsistent reporting makes it hard to track.

      I reviewed the protocols between municipal stormwater systems and public utilities, mapped contact coverage and infrastructure locations so they could later be added to GIS, and summarized interviews with several agencies in a formal deliverable for the department. I ended with recommendations for process changes that would tie environmental compliance to planning documentation under the County's NPDES obligations.

      What came out of it

      Most of what I produced were tools people used day to day: GIS dashboards and tracking systems for site activity and compliance, standard governance templates used across projects, and outreach materials and campaign evaluations for residents and HOAs.

      The TO39 study produced a formal deliverable for the County of San Diego's Watershed Protection Department, a map of contact coverage and infrastructure locations, and recommendations for making pump-out reporting more consistent and transparent.

      In both cases the aim was to reduce nonpoint source pollution and to connect public works and stormwater efforts to the region's larger sustainability and development goals.

      Limitations and next steps

      The hardest part of stormwater outreach is showing that it worked. Participation and reach are easy to count, but research shows that few campaigns compare behavior against a control group. One next step would be to pair a campaign like pesticide reduction with before-and-after behavior surveys in matched neighborhoods.

      Coordinating across jurisdictions also depends on shared data. Each agency keeps records in its own systems, and the dashboards can only be as good as the data that goes into them. The TO39 recommendations suggest common reporting formats and GIS integration as a longer-term fix.

      I'd also like to study an equity question: whether outreach reaches renters, people who don't speak English and neighborhoods without HOAs as well as it reaches organized homeowners.

      Case studies

      • San Diego County, CaliforniaProject Clean Water

        The 21 San Diego Region stormwater copermittees run a shared regional clearinghouse for watershed management areas from South Orange County to the Tijuana River. They also do joint outreach, such as 52 Ways to Love H2O and youth Stormwater Stewards programs.

        Lesson for this project: A regional clearinghouse lets many agencies share one public presence and one set of resources, which is the kind of coordination that compliance across several cities needs.

        Source
      • Orange County, CaliforniaH2OC, the Orange County Stormwater Program

        H2OC publishes pollution prevention materials that residents and businesses across the county can use, on topics like runoff, landscaping, pet care and household hazardous waste. Many are available in Spanish, Vietnamese, Korean and Chinese.

        Lesson for this project: Shared materials in several languages let each city reach more residents without having to build its own campaign from scratch.

        Source
      • Los Angeles County, CaliforniaSafe, Clean Water Program

        Voters approved the program in 2018. It funds stormwater capture and water quality projects through municipal, regional and district shares, and shows the projects on a public online map.

        Lesson for this project: Dedicated funding and a public project map let people see where stormwater money goes. That's a useful model for the tracking dashboards I built.

        Source

      Senior thesis in urban technology and policy, UC San Diego Urban Expo

      Defining A.I. Urban Dynamics: The Role of A.I. Urban Intelligence

      My senior thesis looked at how cities are starting to use artificial intelligence in planning, and what governance, transparency and inclusion should look like when they do. It placed 3rd at the UC San Diego Urban Expo.

      Algorithms that decide where a city's attention goes

      An algorithm that routes inspections, ranks requests or flags risk can look like a purely technical tool, but it also decides where public attention and money go. Cities are starting to use AI and machine learning in planning and public services, often before they have rules for it.

      Some cities are already dealing with this. In September 2020, Amsterdam and Helsinki launched public registers of the algorithms and AI systems they use. In Toronto, residents and advocates objected to the data collection Sidewalk Labs planned for Quayside, and the project was cancelled in May 2020, citing the economic effects of COVID-19.

      My senior thesis (3rd place at the UC San Diego Urban Expo) asked how cities are bringing AI into planning practice. I looked at it in terms of governance, transparency and inclusion: who makes the decisions, who can see how a system works, and whose needs shape the design.

      Role
      Student researcher, UC San Diego Urban Studies & Planning
      When
      Senior thesis, UC San Diego Urban Expo
      Status
      Completed (senior thesis poster)
      Methods
      Practitioner interviews, Review of commercial AI and machine-learning platforms, Spatial analysis, Policy research
      Tools and data
      ArcGIS StoryMaps, GIS

      The research question

      My senior thesis, Defining A.I. Urban Dynamics: The Role of A.I. Urban Intelligence, asked how cities are bringing AI and machine learning into planning practice, often before they have rules for using them.

      I used three lenses that come up again and again in smart-city debates. Governance is about who decides, transparency is about who can see how a system works, and inclusion is about whose needs shape the design.

      These lenses tie into the question behind most of my work, which is who gets what in cities. When an algorithm routes inspections or ranks requests, it is deciding how public attention and resources get handed out. This project is where my GeoAI for Cities series started.

      Background reading

      The thesis builds on work that treats the smart city as a governance question as much as a technical one. Three sources shaped how I framed it.

      • Michael Batty (2018), in an editorial for Environment and Planning B, argues that AI will disrupt urban planning and design without dismantling them, and that planners need to build these tools into their own methods instead of resisting them. My thesis picks up that question from the practitioner's side.
      • Rob Kitchin (2014), in GeoJournal, examines the real-time city built on streams of urban data. He weighs promised gains in efficiency and transparency against concerns that include surveillance, corporate control of city systems and technical vulnerability. Those concerns line up with my governance and transparency lenses.
      • UN-Habitat and Mila (2022), in AI and Cities: Risks, Applications and Governance, warn that using AI without governance mechanisms and attention to human rights can have negative, even catastrophic, effects. The report gives local governments practical recommendations, which makes it a useful checklist for the inclusion question.

      Methods

      My records from this thesis are thin, so I only describe the method at the level they support. The work had three parts, and I presented the results as a poster.

      • Interviews with planning practitioners about how AI is entering their work.
      • A review of commercial AI and machine-learning platforms offered to cities.
      • Spatial analysis, presented as an ArcGIS StoryMap alongside the poster.

      What came out of it

      The poster placed 3rd at the UC San Diego Urban Expo.

      What it mainly contributed was a way of framing the issue. It treats AI adoption in cities as a matter of governance, transparency and inclusion as well as technical capability, and asks practitioners and vendors to account for all three.

      I kept using that framing. The GeoAI for Cities series picks up the same questions about how spatial data and AI shape the way public resources are distributed.

      Limits and next steps

      This was an undergraduate thesis. The interviews and platform review describe practice at one moment, and they do not measure how AI tools changed outcomes for residents.

      Since then, cities have built concrete transparency tools, such as public algorithm registers and review task forces, which make the question easier to test. Next I would compare cities that publish algorithm registers with cities that do not, and ask whether disclosure changes which systems get adopted and who they affect.

      Closer to home, I would inventory how agencies in the San Diego region disclose automated decision systems, and map which neighborhoods those systems touch most.

      Case studies

      • Amsterdam, Netherlands and Helsinki, FinlandAlgorithm registers in Amsterdam and Helsinki

        In September 2020 both cities launched public registers of the algorithms and AI systems they use. Amsterdam's first entries included automated parking control, a holiday-rental fraud risk tool and a public-space issue reporting system, with each entry describing data used, human oversight and how discrimination is prevented.

        Lesson for this project: A register gives residents something they can check one entry at a time, which makes the transparency lens concrete.

        Source
      • New York City, NYAutomated Decision Systems Task Force

        Local Law 49 of 2018 created a task force to recommend a process for reviewing the City's use of automated decision systems, with members from agencies, the private sector, nonprofits, advocates and researchers. It released its report on November 19, 2019.

        Lesson for this project: A city can legislate a review process for algorithms, and the task force model puts agencies and affected communities at the same table.

        Source
      • Toronto, Ontario, CanadaSidewalk Labs Quayside

        Sidewalk Labs cancelled its smart-city development on Toronto's Quayside waterfront in May 2020, citing the economic effects of COVID-19, after the site had been cut from 190 acres to 12. Residents and advocates had objected to the data collection the project planned.

        Lesson for this project: Public trust in how data will be governed shapes whether a smart-city project moves forward, alongside financing.

        Source

      Sources

      1. Batty, M. (2018). Artificial intelligence and smart cities. Environment and Planning B: Urban Analytics and City Science, 45(1), 3-6. Link
      2. American Planning Association. Summary of Batty, Artificial Intelligence and Smart Cities. APA Knowledgebase. Link
      3. Kitchin, R. (2014). The real-time city? Big data and smart urbanism. GeoJournal, 79(1). Link
      4. UN-Habitat and Mila (2022). AI and Cities: Risks, Applications and Governance. UN-Habitat. Link
      5. City of New York. Automated Decision Systems Task Force (Local Law 49 of 2018) and report, November 2019. Link
      6. AI-Regulation.com (2020). Amsterdam and Helsinki launch algorithm and AI register. Link

      Research proposal in urban technology and policy, Urban Studies & Planning

      Eyes in the Sky: Drones, AI, and Without Limitation

      A research proposal and literature review on how drones paired with AI are changing practice on the ground, and what rules should govern their growing use for aerial surveillance.

      Drones in policing, disaster response and farming

      Chula Vista Police Department launched its Drone as First Responder program on October 22, 2018. Its drones launch to 911 calls before officers arrive. Coverage of a 2023 ACLU report notes roughly 1,400 of 18,000 U.S. law enforcement agencies operating drones, some flying to minor calls.

      Drones also do useful work. After Hurricane Irma in September 2017, the FAA issued 132 airspace authorizations for drones to government agencies and critical infrastructure providers, which inspected roads, bridges, cell towers and power plants. A 2024 review of drone crop spraying reports that AI and precision systems cut pesticide use by up to 30 percent of the recommended dose in some cases.

      This proposal looks at those uses side by side. No interviews, surveys or models have been completed yet. It asks how drone-AI technologies are providing novel views that transform practices on the ground, and how they should be governed.

      Role
      Researcher and proposal author
      When
      Research proposal, Urban Studies & Planning
      Status
      Proposal
      Methods
      Literature review, Case studies (proposed): agriculture, disaster response, environmental monitoring, Geospatial modeling (proposed), Expert interviews (proposed), Public surveys (proposed)

      The research question

      Drones combined with AI and better imaging give new aerial views of human activity. The project asks how drone-AI technologies are providing novel views that transform practices on the ground.

      This matters for cities because the same aircraft that maps crop stress or storm damage can also watch a street. Who flies, over whom and under what rules affects who gets protected and who gets watched.

      The aim is to inform policy. Laying out the benefits and risks next to each other should help cities write rules that point these tools toward uses the public benefits from.

      Regulation and prior research

      The proposal draws on federal regulation, civil liberties research and applied studies. These are the sources I'd point a reader to first.

      • FAA Part 107 governs commercial flights of small drones under 55 pounds. Pilots need a Remote Pilot Certificate, and flying beyond visual line of sight requires a waiver. That waiver process is where much of the expansion in public safety drone use happens.
      • The FAA Remote ID rule, published January 15, 2021, requires most registered drones to broadcast identification and location. Operators had to comply by September 16, 2023, and the FAA extended enforcement discretion to March 16, 2024. The rule makes drones visible to authorities, which raises the question of what the public gets to see.
      • The ACLU report Eye-in-the-Sky Policing Needs Strict Limits (Jay Stanley, 2023) documents the spread of drone as first responder programs. Coverage of the report notes roughly 1,400 of 18,000 U.S. law enforcement agencies operating drones, and some programs flying to minor calls. It recommends limiting flights to serious emergencies and publishing flight data.
      • In agriculture, a 2024 review in the journal Drones (García-Munguía and colleagues) analyzed 100 studies of drone crop spraying. It reports that AI and precision systems cut pesticide use by up to 30 percent of the recommended dose in some cases, while noting the lack of standard testing protocols.

      Study design

      The project is at the proposal stage. Three documents exist: a literature review, a proposal subtitled Humanizing Drone-AI Innovation and Policy, and a data collection and management plan.

      The proposal lays out a mixed-methods design. Apart from the literature review, every part below is still planned.

      • Literature review of research on aerial robotics and machine learning (finished as a draft document).
      • Case studies of drone-AI use in agriculture, disaster response and environmental monitoring.
      • Geospatial modeling to show where and how these applications operate.
      • Expert interviews to add practitioner knowledge to the academic literature.
      • Public surveys to measure attitudes toward increasing drone use.

      What exists so far

      The deliverables to date are the literature review, the written proposal and the data plan. No interviews, surveys or models have been completed, so there are no findings to report yet.

      The design does set up a comparison. Looking at agriculture, disaster response and environmental monitoring together shows that the policy questions change with the setting. A flight over a farm field raises few privacy concerns, and a flight over a neighborhood raises many.

      Limits and next steps

      The scope is too broad. Three sectors plus interviews, surveys and modeling is a lot for one study, and the rules keep changing as the FAA expands beyond-line-of-sight flying.

      If I picked this up now, I would narrow it to one setting: police drone as first responder programs in San Diego County. Chula Vista publishes flight data, which would let me map where drones actually fly and compare that against neighborhood demographics and survey responses on trust.

      Any survey or interview work would go through ethics review first, and the data plan would need clear rules for handling location data about residents.

      Case studies

      • Chula Vista, CaliforniaDrone as First Responder program

        Chula Vista Police Department launched its Drone as First Responder program on October 22, 2018. Drones launch to 911 calls before officers arrive, under FAA beyond-visual-line-of-sight waivers granted in 2019 and expanded in 2021, and the department publishes flight data and bars recording private spaces without a warrant or emergency.

        Lesson for this project: Published flight logs make it possible to study where aerial attention actually lands, which is the governance question this project asks.

        Source
      • FloridaDrones after Hurricane Irma

        After Hurricane Irma in September 2017, the FAA issued 132 airspace authorizations for drones to government agencies and critical infrastructure providers. They inspected roads, bridges, cell towers and power plants and helped insurers survey damage.

        Lesson for this project: Disaster response shows the public benefit, and how quickly airspace rules can change in an emergency.

        Source

      Sources

      1. Federal Aviation Administration. Part 107: Certificated Remote Pilots including Commercial Operators. Link
      2. Federal Aviation Administration. Remote Identification of Drones. Link
      3. Federal Register (2023, September 15). Remote Identification of Unmanned Aircraft: enforcement policy notice, 88 FR (2023-20074). Link
      4. Stanley, J. (2023). Eye-in-the-Sky Policing Needs Strict Limits. American Civil Liberties Union. Link
      5. StateScoop (2023). 'Drones as first responders' programs need guardrails, says ACLU. Link
      6. García-Munguía, A., et al. (2024). A Review of Drone Technology and Operation Processes in Agricultural Crop Spraying. Drones, 8(11), 674. Link
      7. City of Chula Vista Police Department. UAS Drone Program. Link
      8. Nextgov (2017). FAA greenlights drone use in Irma recovery. Link

      Urban technology and policy, USP Senior Sequence 186-187, UC San Diego

      Material Allocation in Urban Ecology

      An early-stage proposal to map San Diego's flows of water, waste, building materials and food with GIS, and to ask which neighborhoods are served well by that infrastructure and which are not.

      Where San Diego's resource facilities are

      Cities take in water, energy, food and construction materials, and they send out waste. Where the facilities that handle those flows are located shapes daily life in every neighborhood, and a refill station, recycling center or food hub is closer to some neighborhoods than others.

      San Diego has set targets for one of these flows. Its June 2015 Zero Waste Plan aims for 75 percent diversion by 2020, 90 percent by 2035 and zero waste by 2040. Its strategies include organics recycling infrastructure and a resource recovery park at Miramar Landfill. Those are physical sites, so they can be mapped.

      This is an early draft proposal, and no mapping has been carried out yet. It asks how GIS can map the current allocation of water, solid waste, construction materials and food in San Diego, and where those flows show spatial inefficiencies and inequities across neighborhoods.

      Role
      Student researcher (draft proposal)
      When
      USP Senior Sequence 186-187, UC San Diego
      Status
      Proposal
      Methods
      Urban metabolism / material flow analysis (proposed), GIS mapping and spatial analysis (proposed), Network analysis for facility siting (proposed), Drone photogrammetry workflow (proposed)
      Tools and data
      City of San Diego Open Data Portal, SANDAG, SanGIS, CalRecycle waste characterization data, EPA WARM, USGS water use and land cover data, Pix4D or DroneDeploy (proposed)

      The research question

      Cities take in huge amounts of water, energy, food and construction materials, and they send out waste. Where those flows go, and where the facilities that handle them sit, shapes daily life in every neighborhood.

      This draft proposal asks how GIS can map the current allocation of key resource flows in San Diego, including water, solid waste, construction materials and food. It aims to find spatial inefficiencies and inequities in how those resources are distributed across neighborhoods.

      So it's a question about who gets what. A refill station, a recycling center or a food hub is a public good with a location, and some neighborhoods are closer to it than others.

      Background reading and data sources

      The proposal draws on urban metabolism research, which treats a city like an organism with inputs, stocks and outputs. The sources below also show how limited the data are.

      • Kennedy, Cuddihy and Engel-Yan (2007), in the Journal of Industrial Ecology, compared the metabolism of eight metropolitan regions on five continents. Most showed rising per-capita use of water, energy and materials. They also note that full metabolism data exist for few cities, and call for standard measurement conventions.
      • EPA's Waste Reduction Model (WARM) compares greenhouse gas emissions, energy savings and economic impacts across source reduction, recycling, composting, anaerobic digestion, combustion and landfilling. It is the tool the proposal names for estimating the climate benefit of different strategies.
      • CalRecycle's waste characterization data break disposal down by business group and material for every California jurisdiction. CalRecycle cautions that local figures are estimates built from statewide study averages and local employment and population rather than from samples taken in each city.
      • USGS publishes water use estimates by category at state and county level, with monthly estimates at the watershed scale for 2000 to 2020. That resolution is coarser than the neighborhood scale this proposal targets.

      Proposed methods

      The proposal outlines a GIS-based material flow analysis for San Diego. Every step below is planned.

      Most of the named data sources exist and are public. The City of San Diego Open Data Portal offers downloadable datasets across city departments. SANDAG provides socioeconomic estimates, forecasts and transportation modeling. SanGIS publishes regional layers such as address points linked to parcel numbers, roads, rights-of-way and transit stops.

      • Map current flows of water, solid waste, construction materials and food, and compare them across neighborhoods.
      • Join flows to population density, zoning, transportation networks, socioeconomic data and built infrastructure.
      • Use network analysis to test better locations for water refill stations, waste transfer stations, local food hubs and recycling centers.
      • Collect site imagery with drones: set ground control points, plan overlapping flight grids, process images into georeferenced orthomosaics and 3D models, then digitize buildings, roads and facilities.
      • Share results through interactive maps and 3D views for planners and sustainability managers.

      What the draft produced

      This is an early outline, and there is no completed study yet. The draft produced a research statement, an inventory of candidate data sources, a step-by-step drone mapping workflow and a list of possible comparison cities.

      The comparison list includes Copenhagen, Amsterdam, Curitiba, Tokyo, Austin, London, Singapore and Masdar City. No mapping, network analysis or flights have been carried out.

      Limits and next steps

      The biggest limit is data resolution. CalRecycle jurisdiction figures are modeled rather than sampled, and USGS water use is reported at county or watershed level, so neighborhood-scale flows would rely on proxies such as parcels, land use and service routes.

      The scope is also too wide. Water, waste, construction materials and food would each be a study of its own, and I would also need to confirm which waste collection data the City actually publishes.

      Next I would start with one flow, solid waste and organics, and tie it to San Diego's Zero Waste Plan. I would map where diversion facilities sit relative to the neighborhoods they serve, then add equity measures from SANDAG data.

      Case studies

      • Amsterdam, NetherlandsAmsterdam Circular Strategy 2020-2025

        Amsterdam's strategy aims to halve the use of primary raw materials by 2030 and become fully circular by 2050. It uses the doughnut model and focuses on three value chains: food and organic waste, consumer goods, and the built environment, with a monitor to track ecological and social impact.

        Lesson for this project: Organizing by value chain and pairing it with a monitor is a workable way to narrow a city-wide material flow study.

        Source
      • London, United KingdomLondon's Circular Economy Route Map

        In June 2017 the London Waste and Recycling Board published a route map covering the built environment, food, textiles, electricals and plastics. It set out more than 100 actions and estimated net benefits of at least 7 billion pounds a year across those sectors by 2036.

        Lesson for this project: A sector-by-sector plan with named actions shows how flow analysis can turn into specific decisions for a city.

        Source
      • San Diego, CaliforniaCity of San Diego Zero Waste Plan

        San Diego's June 2015 Zero Waste Plan targets 75 percent diversion by 2020, 90 percent by 2035 and zero waste by 2040. Strategies include organics recycling infrastructure, minimum diversion requirements for franchise haulers and a resource recovery park at Miramar Landfill.

        Lesson for this project: The plan's facilities and targets give this project a local policy hook and a concrete set of sites to map.

        Source

      Planning and design, UC San Diego design proposal

      Reimagining La Jolla Village Square

      A site analysis and redesign proposal that reconnects a car-oriented shopping center to the new UC San Diego Blue Line trolley with a direct pathway, a split building and a central open space.

      A shopping center next to a new trolley station

      On November 21, 2021, the UC San Diego Blue Line extension opened 11 miles of light rail and nine stations. One of them, Nobel Drive, sits on the western side of La Jolla Village Square.

      The center already has a lot going for it: Ralph's and Trader Joe's for groceries, Best Buy, Marshalls and PetSmart, Club Pilates and La Jolla Fencing Academy, and about ten food tenants, mostly chains. But the whole site is built around parking and laid out for one kind of trip, where you drive in for one errand and leave.

      What's missing is a clear, pleasant walk from the platform into the center. This proposal asks how the site could be reorganized so people arrive on foot and by transit, linger, and support local businesses.

      Role
      Designer and author
      When
      UC San Diego, design proposal
      Status
      Proposal
      Methods
      Site analysis, Tenant and land use inventory, Site diagramming, Implementation planning
      Tools and data
      Site diagrams

      The design question

      La Jolla Village Square is a large shopping center with groceries, big-box stores, restaurants and gyms. It is built around parking, yet it now sits next to a trolley station.

      I asked how the site could be reorganized so people arrive on foot and by transit, linger, and support local businesses, instead of driving in for one errand and leaving.

      The goal was a site diagram and analysis that a property owner, the city and the community could react to.

      Research on retrofitted malls and travel behavior

      Two bodies of work shaped the proposal.

      • Retrofitting suburbia. Ellen Dunham-Jones and June Williamson document how dead or dying malls and strip centers have been rebuilt as walkable, mixed-use places, and also how some fall short, staying cut off by wide arterials or priced out of reach of the people who work there.
      • Built environment and travel. Ewing and Cervero's 2010 meta-analysis found walking responds most to land use mix, intersection density and nearby destinations, and transit use to proximity to transit and street network design. That supports a direct, easy-to-follow path from the station into the center.

      How I analyzed the site

      I started with an inventory of the existing tenants and uses. The center holds grocery anchors (Ralph's, Trader Joe's, Cost Plus World Market), large stores such as Best Buy, Marshalls, Ross and PetSmart, fitness and recreation tenants such as Club Pilates, YogaSIX and La Jolla Fencing Academy, and about ten food tenants, mostly chains.

      I then looked at land use, circulation, public space and architecture, and drew site diagrams for the proposed changes. The plan sets out objectives, design moves, challenges and an implementation sequence.

      Proposed design changes

      The main idea is to bring in local eateries and shops alongside the existing chains, and to make the center somewhere you can walk through and explore.

      None of these changes have been built. They are proposals.

      • Direct pathway to transit: a straight, clear walking route from the center to the trolley area, to ease pedestrian flow and reduce reliance on cars.
      • Building split: divide the existing building into two sections, opening a central space for gatherings, events, arts and dining.
      • Roundabout: a roundabout at the central entry to smooth traffic, mark the entrance and calm vehicle speeds near pedestrians.
      • Community elements: public art, green space, pedestrian paths and gathering areas, with sustainable design and stormwater management.
      • Implementation: feasibility study, detailed design with architects and landscape designers, engagement with residents, businesses and transit authorities, phased construction, and public communication.

      Limits and next steps

      This is a concept. I have not tested traffic flows, costs, leases or zoning, and the stakeholder engagement in the objectives has not yet happened.

      The roundabout and the pedestrian core pull in different directions. Placing vehicle circulation in the center of the open space could undercut the walkable heart the building split is meant to create.

      Next, I would count pedestrians between the station and the center, map walking routes and crossings, and talk with tenants and nearby residents. I would also test a version that keeps cars at the edge and puts the plaza between the station and the stores.

      Case studies

      • La Jolla Village, San Diego, CANobel Drive trolley station

        The UC San Diego Blue Line extension added 11 miles of light rail and nine stations, opening on November 21, 2021. Nobel Drive station sits on the western side of La Jolla Village Square and is reached from the center's northern entrance.

        Lesson for this project: The station is already next door, so what's missing is a clear, pleasant walk from the platform into the center.

        Source
      • Mashpee, MAMashpee Commons

        A failed 1960s strip shopping plaza was master-planned from 1988 into a traditional town center with continuous street frontage, local and national retail, and planned housing including affordable and senior units.

        Lesson for this project: A strip center can become a town center over time if the site is organized around streets and storefronts instead of parking.

        Source
      • Lakewood, COBelmar (former Villa Italia Mall)

        A dead regional mall was replaced with a walkable mixed-use district with a public plaza and restaurant patios, praised by Dunham-Jones as a retrofit success. A later assessment found it still walled off by six-lane avenues and unaffordable for its own retail workers.

        Lesson for this project: Good design inside the site isn't enough. The edges, and here the trolley link, decide whether a retrofit serves the surrounding community.

        Source

      Sources

      3. Planetizen. Retrofitting dead and dying suburban malls: what works? Link

      Current research: working paper, 2026

      Who Gets the Shade? Ranking New York Neighborhoods for Tree Planting

      An original spatial study of New York's 42 health neighborhoods. Tree canopy tracks surface heat, heat emergencies track poverty, and the ranking rule a city picks changes who gets trees first.

      The coolest neighborhood with the most heat emergencies

      On a hot August afternoon in 2009, satellites measured the ground across New York City. Hunts Point–Mott Haven in the South Bronx came in at 98.1 °F, the hottest surfaces of the city's 42 health neighborhoods. Port Richmond, on the north shore of Staten Island, measured 91.5 °F, among the coolest.

      If heat alone made people sick, Port Richmond would be one of the safest places in the city during a heat wave. Instead it has the highest rate of heat-related emergency room visits of all 42 neighborhoods: 15.3 per 100,000 residents, twice the city average of 7.6.

      This study is about that gap. Cities are planting trees and cooling streets, and they have to decide where to start. Most begin with the hottest places. I wanted to check whether heat is the right thing to rank by if the goal is to keep people out of the emergency room.

      Role
      Lead researcher (I chose the question, framing, data and methods, and interpreted the results)
      When
      Working paper, 2026
      Status
      Analysis complete; working paper, not peer reviewed
      Methods
      Global Moran's I and LISA (KNN, k=5, 9,999 permutations), OLS with spatial lag and spatial error comparisons, Random 5-fold vs leave-one-borough-out cross-validation, Comparison of five ranking rules, Sensitivity test with 5,000 random weightings
      Tools and data
      Python (geopandas, PySAL, scikit-learn), NYC Environment & Health Data Portal, UHF 42 neighborhood boundaries
      Read the working paperInteractive mapCode & data on GitHub

      Why the ranking rule matters

      Cities rank neighborhoods to decide where public money goes first. Tree planting is a clear example: every program has to choose where to start, and the order shapes who gets shade this decade and who waits for the next one.

      I wanted to know whether that choice is a technical detail or a policy decision. I asked two questions. How much does the choice of ranking rule change which neighborhoods a planting program serves first, and who lives there? And can a model of heat-related illness be trusted in a borough it was not trained on?

      What we already know about heat, trees and health

      The study builds on four bodies of work, and each one shaped a specific choice in the analysis.

      • Urban heat islands. The U.S. EPA reports that heat islands make daytime temperatures in U.S. cities about 1 to 7 °F higher than outlying areas, and that trees and vegetation cool through shade and transpiration. This is why I modeled surface temperature against canopy first.
      • The NYC Heat Vulnerability Index. The city's own index, published by the Department of Health and Mental Hygiene, combines surface temperature, air-conditioning access, green space and median income. It is a reminder that heat risk is social as well as physical, and it names the two variables my study does not yet have.
      • Tree Equity Score. American Forests scores neighborhoods from 0 to 100 by combining canopy with income, employment, race, surface temperature, health, language, age and building density. It is a working example of an equity-weighted ranking, the kind of rule I compared against simpler ones.
      • Spatial cross-validation. Roberts and colleagues (2017, Ecography) show that random cross-validation overstates performance when data are spatially dependent, and that blocked splits are almost always more appropriate for predicting to new places. I used whole boroughs as blocks.

      Data and methods

      I assembled five public indicators for all 42 United Hospital Fund (UHF) neighborhoods from the NYC Environment & Health Data Portal: surface temperature, tree canopy, vegetation, poverty, and heat-related emergency department visits. Every input is public and the code runs end to end from the raw export.

      I first tested how strongly each indicator clusters in space using Moran's I and local LISA statistics. I then modeled surface temperature against canopy, and heat emergency visits against temperature and poverty, comparing ordinary regression with spatial lag and spatial error models.

      Next I compared five rules for choosing the first ten neighborhoods to plant: heat-first, canopy-gap, health-need, an equity-weighted score, and a need-weighted score with poverty removed. For each, I counted how many of the ten fall in the poorest third of neighborhoods. To see which picks hold up under different weightings, I re-ran the equity score under 5,000 random weightings.

      Finally, I tested a prediction model for heat emergency visits two ways: on random neighborhoods, and on a whole borough the model had never seen.

      • Data check: in the portal export, Bensonhurst-Bay Ridge was filed under the code for Canarsie-Flatlands. I re-keyed it by name and added an automatic check that every code matches its boundary name, so the error cannot recur silently.

      Results: canopy tracks heat, poverty tracks illness

      All five indicators cluster in space, which is why spatial models and spatial validation matter here. The main results are below.

      • Canopy and heat. Each extra point of tree canopy goes with about 0.174 °F lower surface temperature across neighborhoods (R² = 0.425).
      • Illness and poverty. Heat emergency visits track poverty (r = 0.594) much more closely than surface temperature (r = 0.203). Port Richmond on Staten Island has some of the coolest surfaces in the city, at 91.5 °F, but the highest heat emergency rate, 15.3.
      • Ranking rules. Ranking by canopy gap puts 4 of the first 10 neighborhoods in the poorest third. An equity-weighted rule puts 9. A need-weighted rule that leaves poverty out entirely still reaches 8, because need and poverty overlap so strongly.
      • Six neighborhoods are robust priorities. Hunts Point-Mott Haven, Williamsburg-Bushwick, East Harlem, East New York, High Bridge-Morrisania and Bedford Stuyvesant-Crown Heights make the top 10 in more than 90% of the 5,000 random weightings.
      • Predicting a new borough. A linear model scored R² of 0.25 on random 5-fold tests but -0.27 when predicting a borough it had not seen, which is worse than guessing the city average. Staten Island was the hardest borough to predict.

      What the canopy-gap rule picks

      A canopy-gap rule sounds neutral, and it does put trees where trees are missing. But in this data its first ten include Chelsea-Clinton, Greenwich Village-Soho and Gramercy Park-Murray Hill, and their average heat emergency rate (7.36) sits slightly below the city average (7.61), against 11.05 for the equity-weighted ten. The rule a city picks affects who benefits, so I think that choice should be made in public.

      Borrowing a model trained somewhere else

      The cross-validation result matters for any city that wants to borrow a model trained elsewhere. A score that looks fine on random splits can fall apart in the place where you want to use the model.

      How the code was written and checked

      The analysis code was written and run with an AI assistant (Claude, Anthropic) under my direction. I set the question, approved the data and methods, and interpreted the results. An independent AI review caught the neighborhood-coding error before publication, and I am reproducing the analysis myself before citing it formally.

      What this study can't tell us

      This is an ecological, cross-sectional study of 42 coarse neighborhoods. Variables come from different years (2005 to 2017), surface temperature comes from a single Landsat scene from August 2009, and the heat emergency rate is an unweighted mean of yearly age-adjusted rates. It shows associations between places, not causes for people.

      Air-conditioning access and age, two of the main drivers in the city's own Heat Vulnerability Index, are not yet modeled. That likely explains part of the Port Richmond puzzle.

      Next, I plan to repeat the study at census-tract level with current canopy and several summers of satellite data, add air-conditioning access and age, seek faculty review, and submit it as a short paper.

      Case studies

      • New York City, NYCool Neighborhoods NYC

        In 2017 the city launched a $106 million heat program that put $82 million into street tree planting in the South Bronx, Northern Manhattan and Central Brooklyn, neighborhoods identified as disproportionately vulnerable to heat-health risks.

        Lesson for this project: Those targets overlap with this study's robust priorities, which suggests a vulnerability-based rule and an equity-weighted rule point to many of the same places, while a pure canopy-gap rule would not.

        Source
      • Phoenix, AZTree Equity goal and Cool Corridors

        Phoenix set a public goal of Tree Equity by 2030, used American Forests' Tree Equity Score to prioritize planting, and mapped 100 cool corridors in areas with high pedestrian use and low canopy, prioritizing low-income and heat-vulnerable neighborhoods.

        Lesson for this project: Phoenix made its ranking rule explicit and public. In this study, that rule was the choice with the largest effect on who benefits.

        Source

      Sources

      1. U.S. Environmental Protection Agency. Learn About Heat Islands. Link
      2. NYC Department of Health and Mental Hygiene. Heat Vulnerability Index. Environment & Health Data Portal. Link
      3. American Forests. Tree Equity Score. Link
      4. Roberts, D. R., Bahn, V., Ciuti, S., et al. (2017). Cross-validation strategies for data with temporal, spatial, hierarchical, or phylogenetic structure. Ecography 40(8), 913-929. Link
      5. Georgetown Climate Center Adaptation Clearinghouse. Cool Neighborhoods NYC. Link
      6. American Forests (2023). Tree Equity Is Growing in Phoenix. Link
      7. NYC Environment & Health Data Portal, data export (All_EHDP_Data). Link

      Current research: working prototype, 2026

      CurbCall: Resident-Ranked Infrastructure Repairs for San Diego

      A phone-first prototype where San Diego residents photograph a broken sidewalk, pothole or dark street, tick a short checklist, and vote on what each part of the city should fix first.

      85,000 open cases in Get It Done

      In March 2026, San Diego's Get It Done app had about 85,000 open cases. A 72-hour parking complaint took about 14 days to close in Pacific Beach. In Del Mar Mesa, Torrey Highlands and Carmel Mountain, it took about 125.

      Get It Done works like a complaint inbox, where one report becomes one ticket. It can count complaints, but it can't show what residents think matters most, or which neighborhoods are being heard. Research on 311 complaints in Kansas City found that low-income and minority neighborhoods were less likely to report street problems, despite greater measured need. If repairs are ranked by complaint volume, that reporting gap turns into a service gap.

      CurbCall is a prototype I designed in response. Residents photograph a broken sidewalk, pothole or dark street and vote on what each part of the city should fix first. It hasn't been tested with residents yet. The question behind it is this: if residents can report and vote on what to fix first, whose problems get heard, and does that match where the city responds?

      Role
      Product lead (concept, feature design, user flow and research framing)
      When
      Working prototype, 2026
      Status
      Prototype, not yet tested with residents
      Methods
      Product and user-flow design, Equity-aware ranking design (per-area rankings), Spatial database design, Planned comparison with Get It Done response times
      Tools and data
      Web app with shared database, PostgreSQL/PostGIS (design), Web mapping
      Open the prototypeCode & database on GitHub

      The research question

      CurbCall asks whose problems get heard when residents can report and vote on what to fix first, and whether their priorities match where the city responds. It's the product side of the question behind my research, who gets what in cities.

      San Diego's own reporting app, Get It Done, works like a complaint inbox: one report becomes one ticket. In March 2026 it had nearly 85,000 open cases, and closure times varied widely by neighborhood. An inbox can count complaints, but it cannot show what residents think matters most, why, or which neighborhoods are being heard.

      Research on 311 reporting

      Three lines of research shaped the design, and each points to a risk a reporting tool has to plan for.

      • Bias in 311 data. Kontokosta and Hong (2021, Sustainable Cities and Society) studied complaints in Kansas City and found that low-income and minority neighborhoods were less likely to report street condition or nuisance issues, despite greater measured need. If a city ranks repairs by complaint volume, that gap becomes a service gap. This is why CurbCall ranks within areas rather than only citywide.
      • Coproduction and the digital divide. Clark, Brudney and Jang (2013, Public Administration Review) treat 311 reporting as citizens coproducing public services. In Boston they found lower-income neighborhoods used 311 less overall, though smartphone requests were more evenly spread. This is why I designed for phones first and planned ways to take part without a smartphone.
      • Participatory budgeting. New York City Council's participatory budgeting has let residents vote directly on capital projects since 2011. It shows that residents can rank public spending, and that turnout and language access decide whose priorities count.

      How the prototype works

      CurbCall is a working web prototype covering all of San Diego, with 124 neighborhoods grouped into 7 areas. Using it takes three steps.

      • Report. Take a photo, drop a pin, pick a category and tick a short infrastructure checklist.
      • Vote. Swipe right to fix it, left if it can wait, and give a reason: safety, accessibility, kids and schools, flooding, or heat.
      • See the ranking. A city view ranks reports by net support within each of seven areas, from North to South Bay, so busy neighborhoods do not drown out quieter ones.

      Design choices

      Most of the work was deciding what the tool should and shouldn't allow. Each choice below responds to a known weakness in complaint-driven systems.

      • A required photo and a short checklist, so every report is comparable rather than free text.
      • One vote per person per report, with reasons, so city staff see the reasons along with the count.
      • Rankings within each area as well as citywide, so neighborhoods that report less aren't ranked last by default.
      • A light, familiar look modeled on apps people already use, so it does not feel like a government form.
      • Planned support for Spanish, Tagalog and Vietnamese, and ways to take part without a smartphone.

      Current status

      The prototype works end to end, but it has no real users yet. The 17 reports in the app are labeled examples for demonstration, so nothing here is a finding about San Diego residents.

      The research part would come next. Paired with Get It Done response times, CurbCall could show where residents are waiting longest and whose voices the city hears.

      The database is designed around PostgreSQL and PostGIS, so every report carries a location that can be joined to neighborhoods, areas and city service records. That spatial structure is what would let the tool compare what residents rank first with what the city actually closes first.

      The comparison I want to make is this: if the neighborhoods that vote most urgently for a repair are also the ones waiting longest under Get It Done, that is evidence the current inbox is not hearing them.

      How it was built

      The app, database and repository were built with an AI assistant (Claude, Anthropic) from my product direction across several design rounds. I set the concept, features, user flow and research framing.

      Limits and next steps

      Voting tools can repeat the bias they are meant to fix. People with more time, better connectivity and more trust in government will vote more, and per-area rankings soften that but do not remove it.

      A required photo also raises the bar to take part. It makes reports comparable, but it may exclude people without a camera phone, which is why the planned non-smartphone options matter.

      A ranking is also not a budget. Residents can say what matters, but the city still decides what it can afford and what is legally required, so the tool should inform repair decisions rather than set them.

      Next, I plan to pilot with community partners in Southeast San Diego, Mid-City and South Bay, write consent language and complete an ethics (IRB) check before collecting any research data, and add before-and-after photos with progress tracking from Reported to Fixed.

      Case studies

      • San Diego, CAGet It Done backlog

        The city's service request app had about 85,000 open cases in March 2026. Hoodline reported 72-hour parking complaints taking about 14 days to close in Pacific Beach but about 125 days in Del Mar Mesa, Torrey Highlands and Carmel Mountain, with hundreds pending in Southeastern San Diego, Skyline-Paradise Hills and Encanto.

        Lesson for this project: An inbox records demand but not priority, and response times differ by neighborhood, which is the gap CurbCall is designed to make visible.

        Source
      • United Kingdom (also deployed abroad)FixMyStreet

        Run by the UK charity mySociety (under that name since 2007), FixMyStreet maps reports of potholes, broken lights and similar problems and sends them to the responsible council, and its open-source platform is used in places such as Zurich and Sweden.

        Lesson for this project: Public, mapped reports and open code show that a reporting tool can be transparent and portable, which CurbCall should match.

        Source
      • New York City, NYNYC Participatory Budgeting

        Since 2011, residents aged 11 and up have voted on capital projects in participating Council districts. In the FY 2027 cycle, nearly 130,000 people in 22 districts allocated almost $25 million, with ballots in 12 languages and over 100 in-person sites.

        Lesson for this project: Resident voting gains legitimacy when it is tied to real money and reaches people through many languages and in-person options.

        Source

      Sources

      1. Kontokosta, C. E., and Hong, B. (2021). Bias in smart city governance: How socio-spatial disparities in 311 complaint behavior impact the fairness of data-driven decisions. Sustainable Cities and Society 64, 102503. Link
      2. Clark, B. Y., Brudney, J. L., and Jang, S.-G. (2013). Coproduction of Government Services and the New Information Technology: Investigating the Distributional Biases. Public Administration Review 73(5), 687-701. Link
      3. Hoodline (March 2026). San Diego's Get It Done app drowning in 85,000 complaints. Link
      4. City of San Diego. Get It Done. Link
      5. mySociety. FixMyStreet Platform. Link
      6. New York City Council (2026). Participatory Budgeting FY 2027 results press release. Link

      Current research, ongoing in 2026

      GeoAI for Cities: Research Series and Website

      A research website and article series on GeoAI and how cities make decisions. It includes an academic primer, an exploratory Manhattan case study and original studies such as Who Gets the Shade?

      What changes when a ranking is called AI

      Imagine two tools that rank the same neighborhoods with the same data. A planner wrote one of them by hand, and the other is called AI. The second can sound more objective, even though the ranking is the same.

      That's one risk of a term people use in very different ways. Vendors, labs and city agencies apply GeoAI to everything from detecting buildings in satellite images to ranking neighborhoods for services. The ranking rule itself matters too. In Part 2 of this series, changing the rule decided whether 4 or 9 of the first 10 neighborhoods picked for tree planting were among the poorest.

      In this series I try to define GeoAI carefully, trace how cities used spatial technology long before the term existed, and keep coming back to who benefits when cities use these tools to rank and decide.

      Role
      Author and editor (topics, framing and research direction)
      When
      Ongoing, 2026
      Status
      Ongoing
      Methods
      Literature and history review, Exploratory case study, Original spatial analysis (Part 2), Interactive web mapping, Science communication
      Tools and data
      Research website, Interactive maps and figures
      Browse the seriesManhattan, MeasuredWebsite sourceShared database

      Why GeoAI needs a careful definition

      GeoAI is a popular term with a vague meaning. Vendors, labs and city agencies use it for very different things, from detecting buildings in satellite images to ranking neighborhoods for services.

      That vagueness matters for cities. When a tool is called AI, it can sound more objective than a rule a planner wrote by hand, even when it is ranking the same places with the same data.

      I wanted a public body of work that defines GeoAI carefully, shows how cities used spatial technology long before the term existed, and asks the question I care about most: when cities use these tools to rank and decide, who benefits?

      Background: GIScience, GeoAI definitions and Local Law 49

      The series draws on two academic traditions and one policy debate. Together they frame GeoAI as a continuation of GIScience, with new consequences for how cities are governed.

      • GIScience. Michael Goodchild's 1992 paper in the International Journal of Geographical Information Systems argued that GIS needed to become a science, not only a system, with spatial analysis at its core. The series treats GeoAI as the latest chapter in that argument rather than a clean break.
      • Defining GeoAI. Janowicz, Gao, McKenzie, Hu and Bhaduri (2020, IJGIS) describe GeoAI as spatially explicit artificial intelligence and ask whether it only applies general AI or contributes something distinct. Industry definitions, such as Esri's description of AI fused with geospatial data, science and technology, are broader. Part 1 sets these side by side.
      • Algorithmic accountability in cities. New York City's Automated Decision Systems Task Force, created by Local Law 49 of 2018, recommended that agencies report on high-priority systems and assess them for disproportionate impacts. That framing, that a ranking system is a public decision, runs through every part of the series.

      What the series includes so far

      The series has three pieces so far. I wrote each one for a general reader while trying to keep the detail an academic reader would expect.

      • Part 1: What Is GeoAI? An academic-style primer with definitions, tables, a timeline of GIS and spatial technology, and paths for both industry practitioners and academics.
      • Manhattan, Measured. An exploratory case study, with case studies and timelines of how researchers measured the city before and after machine learning.
      • Part 2: Who Gets the Shade? An original spatial study of tree planting and heat in New York, with an interactive map where readers scratch away the heat map to see where people get sick.

      My role and approach

      I chose the topics, set the framing, and decided which questions each piece had to answer. I rejected drafts that felt generic, because I wanted the series to say something specific about cities instead of summarizing the field.

      The history matters as much as the methods. Cities were mapping need, risk and service long before machine learning, and many of the equity questions people now ask about AI were already present in older tools like overlay maps and indicator rankings.

      Each piece ties back to who gets what in cities. The primer defines the tools and the Manhattan piece shows how measurement has changed. The shade study tests what happens when a ranking rule decides who benefits.

      Writing, figures and the website were drafted with an AI assistant (Claude, Anthropic) under my editorial direction. Background articles are being fact-checked against sources before formal citation.

      What the series has produced

      The series is still a work in progress. Through it I've practiced explaining technical ideas to a general audience, and gone from defining a term to an original study built on public data.

      Part 2 is the first piece of original research in the series. It found that the choice of ranking rule changes whether 4 or 9 of the first 10 neighborhoods for tree planting are among the poorest, which bears directly on the accountability debate.

      It also showed that a heat-illness model which looked useful on random test splits did worse than guessing the average when asked to predict a borough it had not seen. That's a practical caution for any city that wants to borrow a model trained somewhere else.

      Limits and next steps

      The background articles are not yet fully fact-checked or formally cited, and nothing in the series is peer reviewed. Until that work is done, readers should treat the primer and the Manhattan piece as drafts.

      Next, I plan to fact-check and cite all background articles, add a research statement page and a disclosure note in the site footer, and publish Part 3.

      Case studies

      • New York City, NYAutomated Decision Systems Task Force

        Local Law 49 of 2018 created a task force to recommend how the city should review its automated decision systems. Its November 2019 report called for a central management function, public education, agency reporting on high-priority systems, and checks for disproportionate impacts, and it openly recorded disagreement about how much authority oversight should have.

        Lesson for this project: Defining which systems count and who reviews them is the hard part, so the series should be precise about which spatial tools it calls GeoAI.

        Source
      • Amsterdam, Netherlands and Helsinki, FinlandPublic algorithm registers

        In September 2020 both cities launched public registers explaining the algorithms they use. Amsterdam's listed automated parking control, holiday-rental fraud risk assessment and a public-space issue reporting system; Helsinki's listed service chatbots and a library book recommender.

        Lesson for this project: A plain-language public register is a practical model for the disclosure a city should give residents about spatial ranking tools.

        Source
